info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: open_targets_search
info.description:
Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

Adds new disease-target association data to the state and returns top search results.

disease_names.description:
List of disease names to search for.
Usage:
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Returns top targets for Alzheimer's
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's", "Diabetes"], target_names = ["PSEN1"] ->
    Filters for only PSEN1-Alzheimer's/Diabetes evidence
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab
disease_names.title: Disease Names

target_names.description:
List of target names to search for.
Usage:
target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Returns top diseases associated with BACE1
target_names = ["BACE1", "APP"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for only these target-Alzheimer's pairs
target_names = ["BACE1"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab
target_names.title: Target Names

drug_names.description:
List of drug names to generate or filter results.
Usage:
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Returns all disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names.title: Drug Names

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: paper_search
info.description:
Search for papers in Google Scholar for you to look at.

Can be called repeatedly with identical parameters to retrieve more results (max 2 repeats).
A short summary of the retrieved papers will be returned, but to examine the full content of each paper,
you must use the gather_evidence tool.

query.description:
A Google Scholar search query, which can be a specific phrase, complete sentence,
or general keywords, e.g. 'machine learning for immunology'. Also can be
given search operators like 'author:'.
query.title: Query

min_year.description:
filter for minimum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
min_year.title: Min Year

max_year.description:
filter for maximum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
max_year.title: Max Year

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

Abstract:
A discrete element model (DEM) has been developed for an industrial batch bin blender in which three different types of materials are mixed. The mixing dynamics have been evaluated from a model-based study with respect to the blend critical quality attributes (CQAs) which are relative standard deviation (RSD) and segregation intensity. In the actual industrial setup, a sensor mounted on the blender lid is used to determine the blend composition in this region. A model-based analysis has been used to understand the mixing efficiency in the other zones inside the blender and to determine if the data obtained near the blender-lid region are able to provide a good representation of the overall blend quality. Sub-optimal mixing zones have been identified and other potential sampling locations have been investigated in order to obtain a good approximation of the blend variability. The model has been used to study how the mixing efficiency can be improved by varying the key processing parameters, i.e., blender RPM/speed, fill level/volume and loading order. Both segregation intensity and RSD reduce at a lower fill level and higher blender RPM and are a function of the mixing time. This work demonstrates the use of a model-based approach to improve process knowledge regarding a pharmaceutical mixing process. The model can be used to acquire qualitative information about the influence of different critical process parameters and equipment geometry on the mixing dynamics.

Abstract:
In spite of wide applications of powders in industry, there is a lack of sufficient knowledge regarding the mixing of poly-disperse particles in rotary drum and slant cone mixers. The main objective of this study was to explore the mixing quality of mono-disperse, bi-disperse, tri-disperse, and poly-disperse particles inside rotary drum and slant cone mixers as a function of the drum speed, particle size, agitator speed, and the initial loading method through the discrete element method (DEM). To achieve this objective, experimental work and simulations were carried out. DEM results were validated using experimental data obtained from both sampling and image analysis techniques. DEM simulation results were in good agreement with the experimentally determined data, both qualitatively and quantitatively. Three major loading methods were defined: side-side, top-bottom, and back-front. Also, the mixing metric was utilized to measure the mixing quality. For bi-disperse particles inside the slant cone mixer, the mixing index increased to a maximum and decreased slightly before reaching a plateau at the drum speed of 15 rpm with different loading methods as a direct result of the segregation of particles of different sizes. The same behavior was observed in the rotary drum for bi-disperse, tri-disperse, and poly-disperse particles. The effect of agitator speed on the mixing performance for bi-disperse particles inside the slant cone mixer was also investigated. The addition of the agitator increased the mixing quality and reduced the segregation of particles with different sizes. The best mixing qualities for the tri-disperse and poly-disperse particles inside the rotary drum were recorded for the top-bottom smaller-to-larger loading method. For the slant cone mixer, highest mixing indices for tri-disperse and poly-disperse particles with the top-bottom smaller-to-larger loading method were obtained at drum speeds of 15 and 55 rpm, respectively. The impact of segregation for both mixers was reduced by introducing additional intermediate size particles.

Abstract:
Abstract Advanced Mineral Identification and Characterisation System (AMICS) is based on energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) utilised in a scanning electron microscope (SEM). A specially designed software controls the sample positioning inside the microscope chamber, EDS spectra acquisition and analysis, phase identification, and results visualisation in the form of maps, graphs and tables. Characterisation can be conducted automatically for up to 28 mounted samples in a Hitachi SU3900 SEM with or without coating. Many options exist for an experienced researcher to influence the analysis process: (i) extract a spectrum for each acquisition point and determine chemical composition at this point, (ii) visualise mineral maps for each phase or a group of phases to characterise their interactions, (iii) determine the particle geometry-chemistry relationship, (iv) conduct statistical analysis of EDS spectra, define presence of solute elements, and visualise distribution of particles with a particular chemical composition, (v) manually develop the spectra database for unknown phases and solid solutions. This paper briefly outlines the AMICS software features and selected results for phase characterisation in minerals, metal alloys, and nanoparticle mixtures (MOFs and ZIFs). The influence of data acquisition methodology on accuracy and depth of characterisation is discussed.

Abstract:
Following observations of microcracking in two, out of three, Additive manufactured (AM) 316L steel samples, an investigation was undertaken to ascertain the root cause. Welding diagrams, taking into account composition and process parameters, could not generally account for the experimental observations of non-cracked versus cracked AM 316L samples. EBSD phase maps in all three AM samples exhibited a fully austenitic microstructure not only in the bulk sample but also near-surface. Analysis of microcracked regions in the AM samples showed the presence of local enrichment of Ni, Cu and P. Automated SEM/EDS analysis on feedstock powder samples prepared for cross-section examination revealed a fine, foreign particulate contaminant, expected to arise from NiCrCuP alloy cross-contamination during atomization, to be completely embedded in a 316L powder particle. This type of contamination would not have been revealed on examination of powder mounted onto a SEM stub, a common approach to assess powder quality. Based on this analysis, it is recommended to consider including automated SEM/EDS analysis on powder cross-sections in any standardization protocol for quality control of powders, to increase the chances of detection and identification of fine cross-contaminants. It is also recommended that atomization of NiCrCuP alloy should no longer precede atomization of 316L alloy.

Abstract:
This paper reports the microstructural evolution and mechanical properties of a low-density Al0.3NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) prepared by means of a combination of mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering (SPS). Prior to sintering, the morphology, chemical homogeneity and crystal structures of the powders were thoroughly investigated by varying the milling times to find optimal conditions for densification. The sintered bulk RHEAs were produced with diverse feedstock powder conditions. The microstructural development of the materials was analyzed in terms of phase composition and constitution, chemical homogeneity, and crystallographic properties. Hardness and elastic constants also were measured. The calculation of phase diagrams (CALPHAD) was performed to predict the phase changes in the alloy, and the results were compared with the experiments. Milling time seems to play a significant role in the contamination level of the sintered materials. Even though a protective atmosphere was used in the entire manufacturing process, carbide formation was detected in the sintered bulks as early as after 3 h of powder milling. Oxides were observed after 30 h due to wear of the high-carbon steel milling media and SPS consolidation. Ten hours of milling seems sufficient for achieving an optimal equilibrium between microstructural homogeneity and refinement, high hardness and minimal contamination.

This process involves the mixing of metal powders with other materials such as ceramics or polymers, followed by the application of heat and pressure to produce a solid, dense material. The use of PM has several advantages over traditional manufacturing techniques, including the ability to create complex shapes and the production of materials with improved properties. The novelty of using the PM technique for the preparation of Cu–TiO_2 composite lies in the fact that it enables the production of materials with controlled microstructures and optical properties. The microstructure of the composite can be fine-tuned by controlling the particle size and distribution of the starting powders, as well as the processing parameters such as temperature, pressure, and sintering time. The optical properties of the composite can also be tailored by adjusting the size and distribution of the TiO_2 particles, which can be used to control the absorption and scattering of light. This makes Cu–TiO_2 composites particularly useful for applications such as photocatalysis and solar energy conversion. In summary, the use of Powder Metallurgy for the preparation of Cu–TiO_2 composite is a novel and effective technique for producing materials with controlled microstructures and optical properties. The unique properties of Cu–TiO_2 composites make them attractive for a wide range of applications in various fields, including energy, catalysis, and electronics.

Abstract:
In the last decade, the development of more compact and lightweight radiation detection systems led to their application in handheld and small unmanned systems, particularly air-based platforms. Examples of improvements are: the use of silicon photomultiplier-based scintillators, new scintillating crystals, compact dual-mode detectors (gamma/neutron), data fusion, mobile sensor networks, cooperative detection and search. Gamma cameras and dual-particle cameras are increasingly being used for source location. This study reviews and discusses the research advancements in the field of gamma-ray and neutron measurements using mobile radiation detection systems since the Fukushima nuclear accident. Four scenarios are considered: radiological and nuclear accidents and emergencies; illicit traffic of special nuclear materials and radioactive materials; nuclear, accelerator, targets, and irradiation facilities; and naturally occurring radioactive materials monitoring-related activities. The work presented in this paper aims to: compile and review information on the radiation detection systems, contextual sensors and platforms used for each scenario; assess their advantages and limitations, looking prospectively to new research and challenges in the field; and support the decision making of national radioprotection agencies and response teams in respect to adequate detection system for each scenario. For that, an extensive literature review was conducted.

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The purpose of this study was to investigate how powder fill weight, particle size, and particle size distribution influence force transmission and compaction behavior of powders during compaction within narrow die cavities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Discrete element method simulations were used to model confined powder compaction. Monodisperse and polydisperse systems were analyzed by varying particle size, size distribution breadth, and fill weight. Compaction force–displacement behavior was examined together with particle-level normal, tangential, and cohesive forces, including their axial and radial spatial distributions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Particle size had a stronger influence on force heterogeneity than fill weight within the range examined, with larger particles generating higher and more heterogeneous contact forces. Force distributions were positively skewed, indicating load localization within force chains. Normal and tangential forces were highest near the die wall, reflecting strong confinement effects. While individual particle forces followed similar size-dependent trends across different size distributions, narrow distributions required higher compaction forces due to localized load-bearing structures, whereas wider distributions promoted more uniform force sharing and lower resistance to compaction.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results demonstrated that macroscopic compaction behavior was governed by the organization of force networks rather than particle-scale force magnitudes alone, highlighting the critical roles of particle size, polydispersity, and confinement effects in powder compaction.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

Abstract:
Powder processing and manufacturing operations are rate processes for which the bottleneck is cohesive powder flow. Diversity of material properties, particulate form, and sensitivity to environmental conditions, such as humidity and tribo-electric charging, make its prediction very challenging. However, this is highly desirable particularly when addressing a powder material for which only a small quantity is available. Furthermore, in a number of applications powder flow testing at low stress levels is highly desirable. Characterisation of bulk powder failure for flow initiation (quasi-static) is well established. However, bulk flow parameters are all sensitive to strain rate with which the powder is sheared, but in contrast to quasi-static test methods, there is no shear cell for characterisation of the bulk parameters in the dynamic regime. There are only a handful of instruments available for powder rheometry, in which the bulk resistance to motion can be quantified as a function of the shear strain rate, but the challenge is relating the bulk behaviour to the physical and mechanical properties of constituting particles. A critique of the current state of the art in characterisation and analysis of cohesive powder flow is presented, addressing the effects of cohesion, strain rate, fluid medium drag and particle shape.

## pqac-00000000

From text 'hickey2003aguideto pages 71-74'.

Anthony J. Hickey, Timothy M. Crowder, Margaret D. Louey, and Norman Orr. A guide to pharmaceutical particulate science. ArXiv, Mar 2003. URL: https://doi.org/10.1201/9780203009673, doi:10.1201/9780203009673. This article has 61 citations.

Thief sampling can disturb a static or layered powder bed during insertion, causing interparticle movement, segregation, and contamination of lower bed regions by material from upper layers. Insertion may compact the powder and restrict flow into the sampling chamber, while particle attrition and pressure differences with sampling depth add further error. Sampling bias can also arise from preferential entry of larger, better-flowing excipient particles, electrostatic or size differences, free-flowing particles entering before the probe is opened, and particles becoming trapped around or in the chamber. Consequently, sample results may vary with depth, probe type, chamber orientation, and insertion angle. A core sampler is intended to isolate an undisturbed cylindrical core, and cohesive powders can remain in the tube, but its insertion disrupts powder outside the sampler and its removal further disturbs the surrounding bed. Multiple core locations should therefore be inserted before any sampler is withdrawn, and sampling locations should be separated by at least five core diameters when using a capping device, or two without it, to limit interaction between disturbed regions. These effects are particularly important in layered beds because disturbance and material displacement can mix or redistribute layers and compromise representativeness.

## pqac-00000001

From text 'susana2012lowshearwet pages 106-110'.

L Susana. Low shear wet agglomeration of mineral and metallic powders. Unknown journal, 2012.

Traditional thief samplers can produce biased, nonrepresentative measurements of blend uniformity because their insertion and filling operation disturbs the powder bed. Their cavities open after insertion, allowing powder to flow into them; this intrusion displaces material, creates friction against the probe walls, transmits stresses into the surrounding bed, and generates shear. Consequently, the original structure—particularly any spatial layering—may be rearranged or disrupted, while flow into the cavities can alter the material collected and the apparent mixing degree. The excerpt identifies both external drag on the probe and internal drag within the sampler as sources of disturbance.

The Core Sampler (CS) reduces external drag because it isolates a cylindrical core rather than relying on cavities filling from flowing powder. However, it is not free of error: insertion can deform and compact the sampled core, biasing its composition and spatial profile. Powder displacement and compressive stresses may become large enough to block the probe, preventing complete filling and causing an incomplete or nonrepresentative sample. The CS may therefore disturb layered beds through compaction and deformation even while preserving more of the surrounding structure than a conventional thief. The Sliding Cover Sampler was developed to reduce these effects by sequentially inserting its slide and cover, lowering radial and axial stresses, drag, and compaction.

## pqac-00000002

From text 'susana2012lowshearwet pages 110-114'.

L Susana. Low shear wet agglomeration of mineral and metallic powders. Unknown journal, 2012.

The excerpt identifies several sources of sampling bias and disturbance in powder-blend thief sampling. Probe insertion can compact the powder bed, so the withdrawn core may be shorter than the theoretical volume and may not represent the original local composition. This compaction is quantified by sampling efficiency, the ratio of sampled-core length to insertion depth. In a conventional core sampler (CS), the critical stages are filling during insertion, withdrawal, and emptying; high consolidation stresses can develop, especially during filling and extraction. Wall friction and powder-wall adhesion transmit shear into material beside the probe, producing axial drag and potentially moving material across originally distinct regions or layer interfaces. This is particularly significant in layered beds, where the study used contrasting white lactose and dark cocoa layers to quantify cocoa dragged into the lactose region. The CS also requires piston-driven core extraction, which can create further drag and residual stresses and disturb the sampled structure. The SCS design reduces these errors: its slide-and-cover construction permits the core to be detached by gently tapping the slide before removal, avoiding additional drag and preserving structure. Nevertheless, drag remains possible in both CS and SCS, while SCS geometry, including corners, can create localized narrow confinement and stress buildup. The excerpt does not quantify blend segregation or analytical error beyond these mechanical disturbances.

The excerpt identifies two principal sources of bias and error in thief sampling of powder blends. First, probe insertion can contaminate the collected material with powder from other locations, so the retrieved sample may not represent the concentration at the intended sampling point. Second, components may flow unevenly into the sampler cavity; this can produce biased concentrations, particularly when the blend contains particles of different sizes. These problems are presented as general weaknesses of conventional side-sampling or end-sampling thieves. The article states that the groove sampler and core sampler are more effective, accurate, and reliable than those typical thieves. The core sampler is described as being pushed into the powder by hand or with a threaded rod, with sample size controlled during collection, while powder is scraped into a vial as it emerges. The supplied excerpt does not specifically explain how either sampler disturbs a layered powder bed, nor does it quantify disturbance, layer displacement, or interlayer mixing. It only indicates that probe insertion itself can introduce material from other locations, which could compromise spatial or layer-specific representativeness. Therefore, conclusions about disturbance of layered beds must be limited to this insertion-related contamination mechanism.

Abstract:
The upstream of bioenergy industry has suffered from unreliable operations of granular biomass feedstocks in handling equipment. Computational modeling, including continuum-mechanics models and discrete-particle models, offers insightful understandings and predictive capabilities on the flow of milled biomass and can assist equipment design and optimization. This paper presents a benchmark study on the fidelity of the continuum and discrete modeling approaches for predicting granular biomass flow. We first introduce the constitutive law of the continuum-mechanics model and the contact law of the coarse-grained discrete-particle model, with model parameters calibrated against laboratory characterization tests of the milled loblolly pine. Three classical granular material flow systems (i.e., a lab-scale rotating drum, a pilot-scale hopper, and a full-scale inclined plane) are then simulated using the two models with the same initial and boundary conditions as the physical experiments. The close agreement of the numerical predictions with the experimental measurements on the hopper mass flow rate, the hopper critical outlet width, the material stopping thickness on the inclined plane, and the dynamic angle of repose, clearly indicates that the two methods can capture the critical flow behavior of granular biomass. The qualitative comparison shows that the continuum-mechanics model outperforms in parameterization of materials and wall friction, and large-scale systems, while the discrete-particle model is more preferred for discontinuous flow systems at smaller scales. Industry stakeholders can use these findings as guidance for choosing appropriate numerical tools to model biomass material flow in part of the optimization of material handling equipment in biorefineries.

Abstract:
Background/Objectives: Two fibre optic probes were custom designed to perform Raman and near-infrared spectroscopic measurements. Our long-term objective is to develop a non-destructive tool able to collect data in hard-to-access locations for real-time analysis or diagnostic purposes. This study evaluated the quantitative performances of Probe A and Probe B using model pharmaceutical tablets. Methods: Measurements were performed using pharmaceutical tablets containing hydroxyl propylcellulose, titanium dioxide (anatase), lactose monohydrate, and indomethacin (γ form). Material content and thickness of bilayer samples (samples consisting of a top layer and a bottom layer of differing materials) were also assessed using Probe A to evaluate its capabilities to collect sub-surface information. Principal component analysis and partial least squares regression models were using individual and fused data to evaluate the performances of the different probe configurations. Results: Hydroxymethyl cellulose (RP2=0.98, RMSEP = 2.27% w/w) and lactose monohydrate (RP2=0.97, RMSEP = 2.96% w/w) content were most effectively estimated by near-infrared spectroscopy data collected using Probe A. Titanium dioxide (RP2=0.99, RMSEP = 0.21% w/w) content was most effectively estimated using a combination of 785 nm Raman spectroscopy and near-infrared spectroscopy using Probe B. Indomethacin (RP2=0.97, RMSEP = 1.01% w/w) was best estimated using a low-level fused dataset collected using 0 mm, 2.5 mm, and 5.0 mm lateral offsets of 785 nm spatially offset Raman spectroscopy using Probe A. Conclusions: The different probe configurations were able to reliably collect data and demonstrated robust quantitative performances. These results highlight the advantage of using multiple techniques for analysing different structures.

A Lightweight, Low-Label Framework Towards Autonomous Morphology-Resolved SEM–EDS Analysis in Material Microscopy Valid Text Names: 'deebansok2026alightweightlowlabel pages 1-6', 'deebansok2026alightweightlowlabel pages 6-10', 'deebansok2026alightweightlowlabel pages 10-16', 'deebansok2026alightweightlowlabel pages 16-20', 'deebansok2026alightweightlowlabel pages 20-24', 'deebansok2026alightweightlowlabel pages 24-31', 'deebansok2026alightweightlowlabel pages 31-34', 'deebansok2026alightweightlowlabel pages 34-38', 'deebansok2026alightweightlowlabel pages 38-42', 'deebansok2026alightweightlowlabel pages 42-46', 'deebansok2026alightweightlowlabel pages 46-50', 'deebansok2026alightweightlowlabel pages 50-52' BibTex: @article{deebansok2026alightweightlowlabel, author = "Deebansok, Siraprapha and Limanond, Bannapol and Moraille, Patricia and Boonpalit, Kajiana and Suk-ieam, Kanakorn and Nganpipatmongkon, Visarut and Pakawatpanurut, Pasit and Badia, Antonella and Okatani, Takayuki", title = "A Lightweight, Low-Label Framework Towards Autonomous Morphology-Resolved SEM–EDS Analysis in Material Microscopy", year = "2026", journal = "Unknown journal", month = "Aug", doi = "10.21203/rs.3.rs-10521147/v1", url = "https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10521147/v1", publisher = "Springer Science and Business Media LLC" } Abstract: Abstract

High-throughput materials characterization is essential for self-driving laboratories, yet it is often the slowest and least automated step, largely because extracting meaningful structure–property relationships from complex, multimodal data still requires substantial expert interpretation. This is particularly true for nanomaterials, whose properties are highly sensitive to structure, environment, and measurement conditions. Moreover, extracting statistically meaningful particle-level compositional information, such as chemical heterogeneity and impurity distributions, from paired Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM)–Energy-Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS), remains largely manual and expertise-intensive. Here, we establish a lightweight, data-efficient deep learning framework that integrates directly into SEM–EDS workflows to enable rapid, automated, morphology-resolved particle identification and compositional quantification. To overcome the reliance of existing deep learning methods on large annotated datasets and time-intensive manual labeling, our framework operates with minimal human annotation. Starting from only five fully human-labeled SEM images containing 577 annotated objects, we use a canvas-based strategy to generate a synthetic training dataset comprising approximately 6,000 labeled objects. Training the lightweight model with this augmented dataset yields a mean intersection over union (mIoU) of 0.74, representing a 19.8% relative improvement over training on the experimental images alone. The benefit becomes more pronounced as labeled data grow scarcer: with only two images containing 232 annotated objects, our synthetic augmentation increases mIoU by up to 67%, demonstrating that the pipeline is particularly valuable in the extreme low-data regime. Applied to MXene energy-storage materials, the framework links particle morphology to elemental composition through EDS maps and reveals impurity distributions that remain hidden in conventional field-averaged analyses. The pipeline is designed as a deployable solution that integrates directly into existing SEM–EDS instrumentation without requiring complex architectures or high-performance computing, establishing an accessible route toward autonomous electron microscopy and the broader adoption of deep learning-enabled materials characterization.

M. Rabby", title = "Microplastics Across the Human Body: Occurrence, Detection Methodologies, and Distribution in Human Tissues, Organs, and Biological Fluids", year = "2026", journal = "Microplastics", volume = "5", pages = "157", month = "Aug", doi = "10.3390/microplastics5030157", url = "https://doi.org/10.3390/microplastics5030157", publisher = "MDPI AG", issue = "3", issn = "2673-8929" } Abstract: The rapid growth in plastic production and consumption has led to the widespread contamination of the environment with microplastics (MPs), raising increasing concerns about their potential impacts on human health. In recent years, advances in analytical techniques have revealed the presence of MPs in a wide range of human biological samples, suggesting that these particles can enter, circulate within, and accumulate throughout the human body. This narrative review provides a comprehensive overview of the current evidence on the occurrence and distribution of MPs in human tissues, organs, and biological fluids. MPs have been detected in blood, urine, stool, semen, breast milk, amniotic fluid, ocular fluids, and lavage fluids, as well as in several organs and tissues including the lungs, placenta, heart, kidneys, liver, vascular tissues, and reproductive organs. Among the identified polymers, polyethylene (PE), polypropylene (PP), polyethylene terephthalate (PET), polystyrene (PS), and polyvinyl chloride (PVC) are reported most frequently. This narrative review also summarizes the major analytical techniques used for MP detection and characterization, including Raman spectroscopy, μ-FTIR, LDIR spectroscopy, and Py-GC/MS, which highlight their advantages and limitations. Collectively, the available evidence demonstrates that MPs are not confined to the external environment but are now detectable in multiple compartments of the human body, including highly protected biological systems. However, important questions remain regarding their long-term persistence, transport mechanisms, biological fate, and potential health effects. Further methodological standardization and large-scale human studies are needed to better understand the extent of human exposure and the implications of MP accumulation for human health. ## pqac-00000016

From text 'engblom2012segregationofpowder pages 29-33'.

N Engblom. Segregation of powder mixtures in silos with particular reference to dry mineral-based construction materials. Unknown journal, 2012.

The excerpt discusses silo discharge rather than the detailed flow pattern created when powder is initially poured from a container, so it does not establish a single pouring pattern. It distinguishes mass flow, in which the entire silo contents move, from funnel flow, in which stagnant or dead regions remain while material flows through a channel. Funnel flow is commonly associated with more severe segregation, but describing it simply as “first-in-last-out” is explicitly identified as an oversimplification; the actual withdrawal order depends on the flow geometry and material behavior. Regarding preservation of layers, vertical top-to-bottom segregation—such as fine particles accumulating in upper layers during filling—is not necessarily eliminated during mass-flow discharge and may remain at discharge. Thus, vertical layering can be preserved relatively well, particularly when the segregation is aligned vertically. By contrast, horizontal or side-to-side segregation is often reduced in mass flow because material from different radial positions is mixed at the outlet, although velocity gradients near the end of emptying can limit this remixing. Funnel flow generally does not correct radial segregation because different regions remain stagnant or move at different velocities.


---

## pqac-00000017

From text 'engblom2012segregationofpowder pages 69-72'.

N Engblom. Segregation of powder mixtures in silos with particular reference to dry mineral-based construction materials. Unknown journal, 2012.

The excerpt identifies funnel flow as the predominant discharge pattern: tracer tests indicated that it occurred in nearly all small-silo experiments, and rat-holing was also observed in one test. However, the text does not explicitly state that funnel flow produces a strict first-in-last-out sequence. Instead, it describes the discharge as mixing bulk solids from different radial positions and different fill levels. This mixing generated a nearly constant particle-size distribution for most of the discharge, suggesting that vertical and radial material layers were not discharged as completely isolated strata. Differences became pronounced mainly during the final emptying stage: for the low-fines mixture M1, the outflow became depleted in fines, while for high-fines M3 it contained an excess of fines. Material collected at a free-fall distance of approximately 1.25 m was presumed to represent the last material discharged. Thus, vertical layering or filling-induced segregation was only partly preserved during discharge: the bulk composition was relatively uniform through most of the drawdown, but the final material retained a distinct signature of the initial distribution. The excerpt also reports that filling distribution was strongly affected by free-fall distance, so pouring could create radial segregation even when subsequent discharge mixed material substantially.

## pqac-00000018

From text 'engblom2012segregationofpowder pages 56-62'.

N Engblom. Segregation of powder mixtures in silos with particular reference to dry mineral-based construction materials. Unknown journal, 2012.

The excerpt describes discharge from the small silo as funnel flow rather than mass flow: the hopper angle was 60°, below the approximately 71° angle judged necessary for mass flow with mixture S, and the flow pattern was confirmed by observing the powder surface and using tracer objects to establish emptying order. In funnel flow, the central region moves toward the outlet while material near the walls remains or moves later, so the discharge sequence is not a simple uniform plug-flow emptying. The text specifically indicates that fine particles sift downward toward the hopper walls and are withdrawn during the later stages of complete emptying; rolling coarse particles similarly causes the final discharge to be depleted of coarse material. Thus, the excerpt supports a late-discharge enrichment in fines, consistent with a first-in/last-out tendency for material deposited near stagnant wall regions, though it does not provide a complete universal rule for every layer. Vertical compositional layering is not necessarily preserved: filling generated excess fines at the walls, while modified filling with minimal free fall in S3 produced a uniform distribution at one level and much less segregation. The study concludes that filling and discharge patterns were reproduced across scales, but segregation magnitude depended on conditions.

## pqac-00000019

From text 'engblom2012segregationofpowder pages 41-46'.

N Engblom. Segregation of powder mixtures in silos with particular reference to dry mineral-based construction materials. Unknown journal, 2012.

The excerpt describes silo discharge rather than simple pouring from an open container. The investigated silo was intended to have funnel flow in the upper hopper and mass flow in the lower hopper, but the authors judged that it actually discharged in expanded flow because the fluidization plates did not create mass flow throughout the silo. Visual inspection showed that material near the upper hopper walls discharged last. This is consistent with funnel-flow behavior: material in central regions moves toward the outlet earlier, while material near the walls remains behind and is discharged later, producing an approximate first-in-last-out tendency for some regions rather than perfect chronological layering. The experiments showed that fine particles accumulated preferentially near the silo walls during filling and that the final material discharged contained substantially more fines. In the large-scale tests, the last roughly five to ten tons for product L1 and the last one to two tons for L4 were considered segregated. Thus, vertical or spatial layering is not necessarily preserved uniformly during discharge. Material can segregate laterally during filling, and the non-mass-flow pattern can leave wall-adjacent material until the end. In a true mass-flow silo, material from different radial positions at the same fill level would remix at the outlet, reducing abrupt end-of-discharge segregation; funnel or expanded flow preserves spatial differences more strongly.

## pqac-00000020

From text 'hickey2003aguideto pages 74-78'.

Anthony J. Hickey, Timothy M. Crowder, Margaret D. Louey, and Norman Orr. A guide to pharmaceutical particulate science. ArXiv, Mar 2003. URL: https://doi.org/10.1201/9780203009673, doi:10.1201/9780203009673. This article has 61 citations.

The excerpt describes a conical heap and hopper filling pattern rather than explicitly naming funnel flow. As powder is poured onto a heap, a high velocity gradient develops near the surface. Fine particles percolate toward the relatively stationary central region, while coarse particles roll down the outside toward the walls. In a hopper, this produces coarse material near the walls and a fine-material central core. During discharge, the fine particles are released first, followed by the coarse particles rolling down the inverted cone. Thus, the passage documents a discharge sequence associated with heap formation and segregation, but it does not establish a universal first-in-last-out rule for all funnel-flow conditions. It also indicates that pouring causes vertical or spatial size separation rather than preserving the original layering of granular material. The text emphasizes that heap formation is the most frequent cause of size segregation and recommends keeping the powder-bed surface level during filling or reducing the cross-sectional area to minimize it. The excerpt does not quantify how well vertical layers are preserved, nor does it directly compare funnel flow with mass flow. Its evidence instead suggests that pouring substantially rearranges particles according to size, with fines concentrating centrally and coarse particles migrating outward and downward.

## pqac-00000021

From text 'engblom2012segregationofpowder pages 72-76'.

N Engblom. Segregation of powder mixtures in silos with particular reference to dry mineral-based construction materials. Unknown journal, 2012.

The excerpt describes both funnel-flow and mass-flow behavior in silo experiments, rather than a simple container-pouring test. In funnel flow, material near the center moves toward the outlet while material near the walls can remain relatively stationary until later; thus, funnel flow can produce a broadly first-in/last-out tendency for regions near the walls, but the discharge is not a perfectly discrete first-in-last-out sequence. The reported results indicate mixing of bulk solids from different radial positions during discharge, producing a fairly uniform fines content for much of the outflow. However, material distribution near the upper hopper section remains important: the final discharge composition is influenced by the initial distribution there, and fines may increase sharply near complete emptying, particularly when segregation occurred during filling. The excerpt also shows that vertical layering or segregation is not necessarily preserved intact during pouring or discharge. Radial redistribution and flow can partially mix the material, while surface shape, filling history, free-fall distance, particle properties, and segregation strength affect the outcome. For M4, initially uniform material and the absence of apparent sifting produced nearly constant fines content. Strongly segregated mixtures such as M8 and M9 showed increasing fines toward the end, although the timing and magnitude differed. Therefore, vertical compositional structure may influence discharge order, but it is modified rather than simply preserved.

## pqac-00000022

From text 'engblom2012segregationofpowder pages 88-91'.

N Engblom. Segregation of powder mixtures in silos with particular reference to dry mineral-based construction materials. Unknown journal, 2012.

The excerpt does not directly describe the flow pattern formed when powder is poured from a container or quantify how well vertical layering is preserved during pouring. It does, however, provide relevant evidence about subsequent silo discharge. The discharge model treats the material distribution at the level that discharges last as the principal determinant of segregation near the end of emptying. For funnel-flow experiments, the representative wall fines content was measured at the transition between the hopper and the vertical silo section; for mass flow, the last material filled into the silo was used. The author reports that no significant additional segregation mechanisms, such as percolation or sieving, occur during emptying. Although funnel flow and mass flow differ in discharge behavior, the tested model found that the flow pattern itself had a much smaller effect than the material distribution established during filling. Thus, the excerpt is indirectly relevant to a first-in/last-out interpretation: it emphasizes that material deposited at particular regions or levels during filling can control what is discharged last, but it does not explicitly state a universal discharge order or directly assess preservation of vertical layers during pouring. The reported discharge model had only moderate agreement with experiments (R² = 0.70).

## pqac-00000023

From text 'engblom2012segregationofpowder pages 33-36'.

N Engblom. Segregation of powder mixtures in silos with particular reference to dry mineral-based construction materials. Unknown journal, 2012.

The excerpt concerns discharge from silos rather than the initial act of pouring powder from a container, so it does not establish a universal pouring flow pattern or quantify how well vertical layers are preserved. It distinguishes funnel flow from mass flow: in funnel flow, only part of the material moves while other regions remain relatively stagnant, and free-flowing powders can undergo sifting segregation because different regions move at different velocities. This implies that material does not necessarily leave in a simple, perfectly uniform sequence. The text does support a first-in-last-out tendency for material deposited near walls in expanded-flow situations: material placed next to the walls of the upper hopper and lower vertical section is discharged last. If that material has developed horizontal, side-to-side segregation during filling, strong segregation can appear near the end of emptying because the remaining material is no longer mixed. However, this is specifically described for expanded flow and wall-adjacent material, not as a blanket rule that all funnel-flow discharges are first-in-last-out. The excerpt also emphasizes that flow patterns are complex and usually require tracer experiments to determine, so it provides no direct measurement of vertical-layer preservation during pouring.

URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-76633-x, doi:10.1038/s41467-026-76633-x. This article has 5 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt does not provide a statistical power analysis, minimum detectable composition difference, effect-size assumption, variance estimate, significance level, or formal sample-size calculation for particle-by-particle SEM-EDS measurements. It therefore cannot establish how many particles per sample are required to detect a specified composition difference between samples. The reported operational benchmark is that AutoEMX typically collects approximately 100 EDS spectra per sample, with up to five spot spectra acquired from each randomly selected particle. Consequently, the number of analyzed particles may be lower than 100 when multiple spots are collected per particle, but the excerpt does not state the usual or required particle count. Particles larger than 2 micrometers are favored to reduce mass-effect artifacts, and spectra are collected away from particle edges to minimize substrate contamination. A defensible power-based particle number would require pilot or historical particle-level composition data, estimates of within-particle and between-particle variance, the composition difference to be detected, desired statistical power, and the chosen type-I error threshold. These details may be available elsewhere in the full article or supplementary information, but they are absent from the supplied pages.

## pqac-00000025

From text 'aboustait2013innovativepredictionof pages 25-31'.

M Aboustait, Q Hu, R Frazier, Y Zhang, B Tabb, and T Ley. Innovative prediction of fly ash performance in concrete. Unknown journal, 2013.

The excerpt does not provide a statistical power analysis, a formal sample-size calculation, or a stated number of particles per sample required to detect a composition difference between samples using particle-by-particle SEM-EDS. It instead documents measurement repeatability and acquisition conditions. Three identical SEM-AFA scans were performed on a fly-ash stub, with 90 particles successfully matched across all scans after edge-associated particles were removed. Morphological repeatability was high, with coefficients of variation of 0.71% for diameter, 1.47% for area, and 1.05% for perimeter. For EDS, the live time was approximately 5 seconds per particle, and particle counts ranged from 11,000 to 32,000, averaging 16,500 counts. Increasing live time from three to five seconds improved count levels and reduced variation, thereby improving elemental measurement statistics. These results can inform variance and measurement-error estimates for a future power calculation, but they are insufficient to determine the required particles per sample. Such a calculation would require the expected composition difference or effect size, within- and between-sample variability, significance level, desired power, and the statistical model or test planned for the particle-level EDS data.

Abstract:
<jats:p>We use particle simulations to reveal two distinct propulsion mechanisms for a scallop-like swimmer to propel itself in granular media by reciprocally flapping its wings. Based on the discrete element method, we examine the structure, kinematics and contact forces of particles near the swimmer to quantify how jamming manifests as stagnant zones near the swimmer in a frictional granular medium, which are less intense during the opening stroke than the closing. This broken symmetry is quantified by the difference in the number of strong particle contact forces formed during opening and closing, which shows a linear relation with the swimmer’s net displacement across various swimmer and medium configurations, all favouring the opening stroke. We identify a secondary propulsion mechanism in a dynamic regime with significant swimmer inertia, as the flapping period approaches the coasting time for a moving swimmer to come to rest under the medium resistance. In this case, the swimmer’s net displacement is correlated to the ratio between these two time scales, and the swimming direction favours the closing stroke due to the smaller medium resistance as the swimmer coasts with closed wings.</jats:p>

Abstract:
We present a method for predicting forces on a plough – modelled as a flat, rigid plate inclined in the direction of motion – as it moves through a granular bed. Our method combines coarse, but representative, discrete element (DE) simulations with continuum mechanics. We first homogenize the kinematic information obtained from DE simulations to obtain a continuum strain field. The strain field is then combined with an appropriate continuum constitutive law for the granular material being ploughed and linear momentum balance to obtain forces acting on the plough. Our method has the advantage that it does not require (i) detailed DE simulations nor (ii) extensive calibration of grain parameters to match experiments which, in turn, requires significant effort and may be system dependent. Both (i) and (ii) are necessary if forces are to be estimated directly from simulations. We confirm the effectiveness of our approach by comparing our predictions with results from calibrated DE simulations and experiments.

## 4. The 3rd Hutchinson lecture: numerical modelling of forests with uprooting as a nature-based solution to mitigate flow-type landslides

Abstract:
To protect human lives and infrastructure in mountainous regions from flow-type landslides, engineered countermeasures, such as rigid and flexible barriers, are installed along predicted flow paths. Over recent years, research efforts in physical and numerical modelling have helped advance the understanding of impact mechanisms involved and enabled the optimization of the design of engineered solutions. With the advent of sustainable engineering, attention has shifted towards the use and development of nature-based solutions to impede flow-type landslides. A simple nature-based solution is to consider the effects of forests on the mobility of flow-type landslides. However, to leverage forests, the complex flow-stem interactions and effects of uprooting need to be captured. In this paper, details and results of a new GPU-empowered MPM-LSDEM numerical solver that simulates the effects of flows through tree stems that can uproot are presented along with systematic evaluation of the solver. Simulations of flow-forest interaction with and without uprooting show that forests have profound effects on flow forest interaction. For dense forests, uprooted stems can push flow material to enhance its runout distance. Additionally, uprooted stems tend to concentrate near the front of the flows even if they were evenly distributed throughout the model forest at the beginning. The impact force exerted by a stem can be considered concentrated loading and can damage barriers along the flow path. Taken together, hazard assessment tools that can model the effects of uprooting are crucial to close predictions of hazard extent (i.e., runout distance) and the design of physical countermeasures such as barriers.

We conceived, designed and characterized novel thief probes for cohesive powders, that

we called the Sliding Cover Samplers (SCS). They consist of two thin metallic shells to

be inserted sequentially into the bed of powder in order to extract a representative core.

on the powder are minimized reducing both the invasiveness on the bed and the dragging

of material in the sample. The extremity of the probe does not require to be closed since

opened, exposing the sampled core. This procedure reduces therefore the possibility of

segregation (which is associated to flow conditions) and minimize the possibility of

contaminating the sample with material dragged from the upper levels, as quantitatively

proved in this work. SCSs of different shapes and sizes have been tested and compared

with other kind of thief probes (commercial and not). Results showed that SCSs are more

efficient than traditional devices since they reduce significantly both the consolidation

and the drag of the powder. SCSs probes are not limited to any sampling depth,

differently from CS. SCSs probes also allow in a single operation to determine a

This research was mainly concerned with the study of the wet agglomeration of mineral

and metallic powders carried out in low shear mixers. Particularly this work is a practical

The purpose of this study was to investigate the effect of primary particle properties and

process parameters on the finale granule characteristics in order to minimize segregation

mechanisms.

The research activity can be summarized in three main points:

    1.  Wettability study of mineral and  metallic powders by using two  different

A MODENA. Preliminary design of a rotary brush sampler for asteroid regolith collection. Unknown journal, Unknown year.

The excerpt provides general guidance relevant to DEM simulation of a tool or probe interacting with a granular bed, but it does not describe a specific insertion simulation, layered-bed setup, Hertz–Mindlin parameters, or a coarse-graining procedure. DEM represents each grain as an independent body and advances the system through discrete time steps: contacts or overlaps are detected, overlap is interpreted as elastic/plastic deformation, contact laws calculate normal and tangential forces (and potentially resisting moments), and resultant forces and torques are integrated using Newton’s laws. The method is particularly appropriate for asteroid regolith because granular behavior arises from discrete particle rearrangement rather than a continuous stress field, especially under low gravity and low confinement. The excerpt notes that explicit DEM requires small time steps to resolve the stiffest contact, creating computational limits of roughly a few hundred thousand to a few million particles. For angular regolith, realistic polyhedral or clumped-sphere particles are more accurate but substantially more expensive. The approach adopted in the document uses spherical particles with nonlinear rolling-resistance contact formulations to mimic angular-particle interlocking. Specific stiffness, friction, cohesion, damping, restitution, Hertz–Mindlin equations, particle counts for a tool-insertion case, and coarse-graining scaling laws are not included in the supplied passage.
