Abstract:
To protect human lives and infrastructure in mountainous regions from flow-type landslides, engineered countermeasures, such as rigid and flexible barriers, are installed along predicted flow paths. Over recent years, research efforts in physical and numerical modelling have helped advance the understanding of impact mechanisms involved and enabled the optimization of the design of engineered solutions. With the advent of sustainable engineering, attention has shifted towards the use and development of nature-based solutions to impede flow-type landslides. A simple nature-based solution is to consider the effects of forests on the mobility of flow-type landslides. However, to leverage forests, the complex flow-stem interactions and effects of uprooting need to be captured. In this paper, details and results of a new GPU-empowered MPM-LSDEM numerical solver that simulates the effects of flows through tree stems that can uproot are presented along with systematic evaluation of the solver. Simulations of flow-forest interaction with and without uprooting show that forests have profound effects on flow forest interaction. For dense forests, uprooted stems can push flow material to enhance its runout distance. Additionally, uprooted stems tend to concentrate near the front of the flows even if they were evenly distributed throughout the model forest at the beginning. The impact force exerted by a stem can be considered concentrated loading and can damage barriers along the flow path. Taken together, hazard assessment tools that can model the effects of uprooting are crucial to close predictions of hazard extent (i.e., runout distance) and the design of physical countermeasures such as barriers.

Core sampler extraction

After the filling of the CS probe the powder remains consolidated and most of the stresses

leading to the formation of the plug cannot be recovered unless the powder is sheared.

While this allows the safe removal of the sample, without closing the probe extremity,

complication arise to recover the sampled powder, since consolidation prevents any

motion of the material and a piston is required to push out the plugged material (Muzzio,

1999; 2003).


Sample withdrawal from the CS

5.7 Experiments

To highlight the important effects of the stress distribution inside the probe and to

visualize the extent of compaction of the materials inside the CS, before illustrating the

advantages of SCS probes, we carried out a simple preliminary experiment. A bed of

powder with a total depth of 150 mm, was prepared with four layers of equal thickness, of

monohydrate lactose and cocoa powders (dark), as shown in Figure 5.8.





 Figure 5.8 Qualitative (a) and quantitative (b) comparison of bed structure before and after sampling with
                                   a glass Core Sampler


The CS is in this case a transparent glass tube (i.d. 15 mm and o.d. 18 mm) which was

vertically introduced into the stratified bed. The structure of the sample withdrawn by the

glass probe was then compared to the structure of the original bed. Figure 5.8a clearly

shows drag increase with the level of compaction (in particular with radial stresses at the

walls).

5.9 The drag characterization

We compared the two SCS shapes for determining the intensity of material drag during

insertion. We used a sharp material interface and the solidification and slicing technique

described above.

Figure 5.10 shows typical results, with three cross-sections extracted from the solidified

core of a triangular (L = 20 mm) and a semi-cylindrical (D = 10 mm) SCS. Sections are

progressively farther from the cocoa (dark) – lactose (white) interface, illustrating the

carryover of dark powder in the white region.

We immediately perceive that the semi-cylindrical probe reduces drag with respect to the

triangular probe, being lower the amount of dark powder dragged  to the lactose area .

Repeated experiments confirmed that drag in the triangular probe is more intense at the

corners, as apparent form Figure 5.10. Friction in narrower confinements (acute angle

corners) is higher presumably because of a larger local stress, eventually leading to

significant drag. On the contrary, the semi-cylindrical construction reduces narrow angles

and thus the material drag, suggesting that an even better SCS would be obtained by two

semi-cylindrical parts, suitably coupled.Development and characterization of a new thief sampling device for cohesive powders              103

quantitatively the penetration of contamination across a sharp composition interface, due

5.10 Conclusions

We conceived, designed and characterized novel thief probes for cohesive powders, that

we called the Sliding Cover Samplers (SCS). They consist of two thin metallic shells to

be inserted sequentially into the bed of powder in order to extract a representative core.

Because of the thin profile of the shells and of the particular insertion procedure, stresses

on the powder are minimized reducing both the invasiveness on the bed and the dragging

of material in the sample. The extremity of the probe does not require to be closed since

cohesion prevents the outflow of material from the probe during the extraction. The

advantage of this sampling probes is that powder does not move to enter the probe but it106                                                                                 Chapter 5


is the probe that envelope a static portion of material. Also the final withdrawal of the

core from the probe does not require the powder to move since it is the probe that is

opened, exposing the sampled core. This procedure reduces therefore the possibility of

segregation (which is associated to flow conditions) and minimize the possibility of

contaminating the sample with material dragged from the upper levels, as quantitatively

proved in this work. SCSs of different shapes and sizes have been tested and compared

with other kind of thief probes (commercial and not). Results showed that SCSs are more

efficient than traditional devices since they reduce significantly both the consolidation

and the drag of the powder. SCSs probes are not limited to any sampling depth,

differently from CS. SCSs probes also allow in a single operation to determine a

composition profile along the whole powder bed depth. Considering that SCSs simplify

the probe design and use, they can be considered a viable alternative to commercial thief

probes when dealing with cohesive powders.Development and characterization of a new thief sampling device for cohesive powders              107

 Conclusions and future perspectives



This research was mainly concerned with the study of the wet agglomeration of mineral

and metallic powders carried out in low shear mixers. Particularly this work is a practical

framework of binder granulation which takes place in the process of manufacturing of

welding rods.

The purpose of this study was to investigate the effect of primary particle properties and

process parameters on the finale granule characteristics in order to minimize segregation

mechanisms.

The research activity can be summarized in three main points:

    1.  Wettability study of mineral and  metallic powders by using two  different

       techniques: sessile drop and Washburn’s method. This experimental work has

       allowed us to suggest a general method for characterizing wettability of mineral

      and metallic powders.

    2. An in-depth study of agglomeration of mineral and  metallic powders with

        particular attention to the understanding of nucleation and growth regimes of

       granules by using dimensionless numbers approach; this study was carried out

       both  experimentally  in low  shear  pilot  plant and by means  of numerical

       simulations (DEM, Discrete Element Modelling);

    3.  Development and characterization of sampling tools to collect cohesive powders

        in order to assess chemical composition and degree of segregation of granules

       formed.

Concerning the wettability measurements, it was found that the main weakness in the

sessile drop method is to get reproducible data. The drop penetration behaviour is quite

complex and highly dependent on the structure of powder bed, particularly for a non-ideal

surfaces such as mineral and metallic powders. Drop penetration results are affected by

powder compaction and the porosity at the surface. Furthermore it has been very difficult

to identify the correct instant when the drop penetration starts and this aspect can also

affect the measurements of penetration time and rate.

Concerning Washburn’s experiments, the choice of the best wetting liquid remains a

critical step. This work showed that for mineral and metallic powders the reference

Abstract:
Abstract Flowing granular materials segregate due to differences in particle size (driven by percolation) and density (driven by buoyancy). Modelling the segregation of mixtures of large/heavy particles and small/light particles is challenging due to the opposing effects of the two segregation mechanisms. Using discrete element method (DEM) simulations of combined size and density segregation we show that the segregation velocity is well described by a model that depends linearly on the local shear rate and quadratically on the species concentration for free surface flows. Concentration profiles predicted by incorporating this segregation velocity model into a continuum advection–diffusion–segregation transport model match DEM simulation results well for a wide range of particle size and density ratios. Most surprisingly, the DEM simulations and the segregation velocity model both show that the segregation direction for a range of size and density ratios depends on the local species concentration. This leads to a methodology to determine the combination of particle size ratio, density ratio and particle concentration for which a bidisperse mixture will not segregate.

The excerpt indicates that strong interparticle cohesion is especially important for very fine, soft, or irregular particles, including particles smaller than approximately 20 µm. In fluidization, cohesion can prevent uniform bed expansion: gas forms channels while much of the powder remains stagnant, and plugging or channeling occurs. For mixing, cohesion promotes agglomeration and can prevent individual particles from separating and redistributing. Sufficient energy is needed to break cohesive forces within aggregates; otherwise, low-energy mixers may blend agglomerates rather than individual particles, producing nonuniformity. Interactive mixing can improve homogeneity when fine drug particles adhere to larger carrier particles, creating stable ordered mixtures. However, segregation remains possible if adhered fine particles detach (constituent segregation), or if interactive units differ in size and undergo percolation or trajectory segregation. The excerpt also identifies percolation, densification, vibration, gravity, and particle acceleration as segregation mechanisms in random mixtures. ### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Method | Drag-down contamination | Core shortening / plugging | Layer-boundary smear | Preserves depth order? | Suitability for cohesive 15–63 µm Al powder | Overall rating |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Open glass tube pushed to bottom, sealed, then divided** | Likely appreciable: the open mouth admits powder continuously, while wall friction drags upper material downward. No direct value exists for this exact method; conventional side thieves showed **90% upper-layer material 10 mm below an interface**, and material could originate along the entire insertion path (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000027). | **High risk.** A comparable 15 mm core tube recovered only **60%** of insertion depth. Wall adhesion and friction produce exponentially increasing axial stress and may plug the tube; thumb-sealing does not correct an already shortened core (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027). | Potentially severe and asymmetric—primarily downward during insertion, with further rearrangement during emptying into thirds. Conventional side-sampler experiments found mixed material within **two aperture diameters (3.25 mm)** of an interface (pqac-00000013). | **Poor to fair.** Broad top/middle/bottom order may survive, but equal recovered thirds do not correspond to equal original bed depths when the core shortens. | Cohesion may keep powder in the tube and limit loss, but increases adhesion, plugging, compression, and uncertainty in mapping recovered length to original depth (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000042). | **Not recommended** unless first validated using a visibly layered surrogate and measured core-recovery ratio. |
| **2. Piston corer: plunger held at surface while tube advances, then core extruded** | Among insertion tools, relatively low but nonzero. Comparable core samplers had **<10%** upper-layer contamination 10 mm below an interface, versus **45%** for a blunt slug sampler and **90%** for a side sampler (pqac-00000027). | **Main weakness.** Comparable core efficiency was only **60%**; internal wall friction compresses and can plug the core. Piston extrusion reverses powder motion, can require much greater stress, further compact the sample, and cause reverse drag (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000028). | Usually narrower than an ordinary thief’s, but boundaries are compressed and smeared downward during insertion and potentially upward during extrusion. | **Fair to good if corrected.** A continuous core retains sequence better than thieves, but thirds should be assigned using original-depth calibration rather than assumed from recovered length. | Cohesion helps retain the core but makes plugging and extrusion stress worse. Use a thin-wall, sharp, polished, large-bore tube; extrude slowly and discard narrow boundary slices (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000028). | **Second-best practical option** after layerwise removal; preferable to an open tube or ordinary thief. |
| **3. Multi-compartment commercial or 3D-printed thief** | Strongly design-dependent. Reported maximum composition errors were about **100%** for a commercial side thief, **30%** for a blunt slug/end thief, and **10–20%** for a streamlined pointed end thief. Even the best device collected particles initially **5–10 cm** from the target location; side and slug samplers had **90%** and **45%** upper-layer contamination 10 mm below an interface (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000027). | Side cavities may underfill when cohesive powder cannot flow into them; cavities can also fill before opening. Internal partitions do not prevent disturbance along the insertion path (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013). | Conventional side-sampling produced mixed color within **two aperture diameters (3.25 mm)** of a boundary. Every compartment may sample a sheath already contaminated by insertion drag (pqac-00000013). | **Poor for chronological depth profiling.** Simultaneous nominal depths are attractive, but collected material may represent the insertion path rather than the original local layer. | Particularly unfavorable: cohesion impedes cavity filling, while tribocharging and rough 3D-printed surfaces can increase adhesion. A polished, pointed, gasketed design is better but still inferior to coring or peeling (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000014). | **Generally worst choice** for this objective; acceptable only after powder-specific tracer validation. |
| **4. Remove successive horizontal layers with spatula or spoonula** | **No insertion drag-down.** The principal error is local downward cutting or collecting slumped material from the newly exposed surface; no directly comparable quantitative value was reported. | None. No enclosed core means no wall-friction shortening or plugging. | Usually the smallest controllable smear if thin layers are shaved across the whole cross-section. Smear is set mainly by scoop penetration, surface roughness, and sidewall residue; avoid digging and exclude deliberate wall-brushings from the time series. Surface scooping can otherwise cause particles to flow down a slope and enrich fines (pqac-00000007). | **Best.** Directly maps removed mass or thickness to original depth, provided the container stays upright and each full cross-sectional layer is removed before the next. | Cohesion is beneficial because it suppresses slumping and percolation, although agglomerates and electrostatic adhesion require antistatic tools and gentle handling (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000043). | **Best overall for a shallow, accessible bed.** Prefer full-cross-section mass fractions over three isolated spoonfuls. |
| **5. Pour out while translating the container over a plate** | No probe drag, but discharge itself redistributes material. Funnel flow is only approximately first-in/last-out: central material moves first, wall material later, and material from different radii and heights can mix (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000023). | None, although cohesive powder may discharge in intermittent plugs or leave wall deposits, breaking the depth-to-position mapping. | Potentially broad. A flowing surface avalanche mixes neighboring layers; heap formation also causes fines to percolate inward while coarser particles roll outward (pqac-00000020). | **Unreliable without calibration.** The line records discharge time, not uniquely original depth; strict FIFO or LIFO should not be assumed. Final discharge can be disproportionately wall material (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019). | Cohesion may reduce size segregation and make plug-like discharge more order-preserving, but may instead cause clumps, rat-holing, intermittent release, and retained wall powder. Keep drop height and heap formation minimal (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000045). | **Third choice after peeling and piston coring.** Use only if tracer tests demonstrate a monotonic depth-to-line-position calibration for the actual tube and powder. |


*Table: Comparison of five methods for recovering chronological depth layers from a shallow cohesive powder bed. The evidence favors full-cross-section layer removal, followed by a calibrated piston corer.*

{"answer": "## Preservation of Vertical Layering During Sampling of Shallow Powder Beds: Evidence from Experimental Studies, DEM Frameworks, and Statistical Considerations

### 1. Overview and Literature Landscape

The question of how well sampling tools preserve the chronological (vertical) layering of a powder bed has been addressed most thoroughly in the pharmaceutical blending literature, where blend uniformity testing by thief probes is critical for regulatory compliance. The key experimental studies are by Muzzio et al. (1997), who quantitatively compared side-sampling, end-sampling, and streamlined probes using layered glass-bead beds solidified with gelatin (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014), and Susana (2012), who developed and tested a sliding-cover sampler (SCS) using stratified lactose–cocoa powder beds and measured both sampling efficiency and drag contamination (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028). Funnel-flow and mass-flow discharge order have been studied by Engblom (2012) using tracer objects and composition monitoring during silo emptying (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018). Cohesive powder behavior is reviewed by Hogg (2009) and Hickey et al. (2003) (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000043, pqac-00000045).

A notable finding of this literature search is that **no DEM simulation has been published that directly models the insertion of a thief or core sampler into a layered granular bed** and quantifies boundary smearing or drag-down in particle diameters. DEM studies of granular intruders (ploughs, indentation tools, probes) exist, using Hertz–Mindlin contact mechanics with JKR or linear cohesion models (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034, pqac-00000035), but they have not been applied to the sampling geometry. The quantitative data below therefore come entirely from physical experiments with tracer- or contrast-layered beds.

### 2. Quantitative Evidence for Each Sampling Method

The following table summarizes the key quantitative contamination and efficiency data from the literature:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

The overall comparison of the five proposed sampling approaches is presented below:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

#### Method 1: Open Glass Tube, Thumb-Sealed

No published study uses this exact configuration. #### Method 1: Open Glass Tube, Thumb-Sealed

No published study uses this exact configuration. However, a glass core sampler (15 mm ID) pushed through a 150 mm lactose bed recovered only 60% of the insertion depth due to wall-friction plugging (susana2012lowshearwet pages 114-119, susana2012lowshearwet pages 119-123). The axial stress required to continue filling the tube grows exponentially with depth and is determined by the wall friction coefficient μ_w and the Janssen K-ratio (susana2012lowshearwet pages 114-119). When the tube is open during insertion, powder enters continuously from the bottom; wall friction drags upper material downward, compressing the core. Dividing the shortened core into equal thirds does not correspond to equal original bed depths. For cohesive 15–63 µm powder, the high surface-to-volume ratio increases wall adhesion, making plugging more severe.

#### Method 2: Piston Corer

The piston corer addresses the continuous-entry problem by holding a plunger at the powder surface while the tube is pushed down. This is mechanically similar to the core sampler tested by Susana (2012), which showed <10% contamination of upper-layer material 10 mm below a sharp interface—substantially better than side-sampling thieves (90%) or slug end-samplers (45%) (susana2012lowshearwet pages 119-123). However, core shortening remains a concern: the 60% sampling efficiency measured for a 15 mm core tube means that a 40% compression of the core occurs. During extrusion, the stress required to push out the core can be double that developed during insertion (the exponent effectively doubles), further compacting the sample and potentially inducing reverse drag (susana2012lowshearwet pages 114-119, susana2012lowshearwet pages 123-128). For cohesive powder, wall adhesion a_w contributes an additional exponential term to the stress profile (susana2012lowshearwet pages 114-119). Using a larger-diameter, polished, thin-wall tube reduces stress buildup substantially.

#### Method 3: Multi-Compartment Sampling Thief

The extensive experiments of Muzzio et al. (1997) demonstrate that all thief designs introduce significant errors in layered beds. A commercial side-sampling thief (Globe Pharma) produced samples that were "composed almost entirely of particles from the top layer regardless of whether the top layer was composed of smaller particles or larger particles," with maximum composition errors approaching 100% (muzzio1997samplingpracticesin pages 8-11). Even particles entered the cavity before it was opened. The streamlined Rutgers end-sampling thief still showed ~10% composition error and contamination from particles originally 5–10 cm from the target location (muzzio1997samplingpracticesin pages 11-14). The conventional side-sampling probe produced mixed-color sand within two aperture diameters (3.25 mm) of the layer boundary (muzzio1997samplingpracticesin pages 8-11). For cohesive powders, an additional problem is that material may not flow readily into thief cavities, producing undersized or biased samples (muzzio1997samplingpracticesin pages 7-8).

#### Method 4: Layer-by-Layer Removal with Spatula

This method avoids insertion drag entirely because no probe penetrates the bed. The principal errors are (i) cutting too deep, mixing the current layer with the one below, and (ii) surface segregation during scooping, where fines can percolate through coarser particles on a sloped surface (hickey2003aguideto pages 67-71). For the user's application (a tube a few cm across, total depth a few cm), removing full cross-sectional layers by careful horizontal scraping should give the best depth fidelity. Cohesion is beneficial here: it suppresses particle mobility, reduces slumping of exposed surfaces, and makes the exposed layer more stable (hogg2009mixingandsegregation pages 2-4, hickey2003aguideto pages 74-78).

#### Method 5: Pour-and-Sample Along a Line

Pouring powder from a container involves complex flow patterns. In narrow containers, discharge commonly follows a funnel-flow pattern, which is only approximately first-in-last-out: material near the center exits first while wall-adjacent material exits last (engblom2012segregationofpowder pages 29-33, engblom2012segregationofpowder pages 56-62, engblom2012segregationofpowder pages 41-46). Engblom (2012) found that discharge produced nearly constant fines content for most of the outflow, with strong composition changes only in the final material (engblom2012segregationofpowder pages 69-72, engblom2012segregationofpowder pages 72-76). Critically, pouring onto a surface creates a heap, and heap formation causes size segregation: fines percolate centrally while coarse particles roll outward (hickey2003aguideto pages 74-78). Surface avalanche flow mixes adjacent layers during deposition. The model for discharge segregation showed only moderate agreement with experiments (R² = 0.70) (engblom2012segregationofpowder pages 88-91). For cohesive 15–63 µm powder, discharge may be plug-like (more order-preserving) but could also produce rat-holing or intermittent flow (hogg2009mixingandsegregation pages 4-5).

### 3. DEM Contact Models and Simulation Framework

While no DEM simulation has been published for sampling tool insertion into layered beds, the relevant framework is well established. The standard contact model is the **Hertz–Mindlin no-slip formulation**: normal forces depend nonlinearly on elastic overlap through the effective Young's modulus and effective radius (Hertzian contact), while tangential forces use Mindlin's incremental stiffness with Coulomb friction limiting (knight2019fluidflowand pages 77-82, knight2019fluidflowand pages 74-77). For cohesive powders, the **Johnson–Kendall–Roberts (JKR) model** is typically added to introduce adhesion, with pull-off forces proportional to surface energy and particle radius; this is implemented in common DEM packages such as EDEM 2.7.1 (behjani2018numericalsimulationof pages 79-83). The Rayleigh timestep criterion (typically 20–40% of the critical value) governs simulation stability (behjani2018numericalsimulationof pages 79-83). Practical DEM simulations can handle several hundred thousand to a few million particles (modenaUnknownyearpreliminarydesignof pages 62-65, modenaUnknownyearpreliminarydesignofa pages 62-65); for the user's application (a tube a few cm across containing ~5–100 g of 15–63 µm powder), the particle count would be on the order of 10⁶–10⁸, which is at the limit of current capability and would require coarse-graining (e.g., particle upscaling by a factor of 3–10, with adjusted contact parameters to preserve bulk behavior).

### 4. How Conclusions Change for Cohesive 15–63 µm Aluminium Powder

The user's powder spans a size range where interparticle cohesion becomes significant. Particles below ~20 µm are strongly cohesive, with dry-powder cohesion reducing individual-particle mobility and promoting agglomerate formation (hogg2009mixingandsegregation pages 4-5). For the full 15–63 µm distribution, the key changes relative to the literature experiments (which used free-flowing glass beads or lactose) are:

- **Reduced segregation:** Cohesion suppresses percolation and trajectory segregation mechanisms, meaning the as-deposited layering should be better preserved during storage (hogg2009mixingandsegregation pages 2-4, hickey2003aguideto pages 74-78). This is favorable for the user's objective.
- **Increased plugging risk in core samplers:** Wall adhesion a_w adds an exponential term to the stress buildup inside the probe, reducing sampling efficiency below the already-low 60% measured for lactose (susana2012lowshearwet pages 114-119). A polished, large-bore stainless or PTFE-lined tube is advisable.
- **Thief cavity underfilling:** Cohesive powders may not flow into thief cavities, producing undersized or unrepresentative samples (muzzio1997samplingpracticesin pages 7-8).
- **Layer-by-layer removal is more stable:** Cohesion prevents the exposed surface from slumping or self-segregating, making spatula removal the most reliable method (hogg2009mixingandsegregation pages 2-4).
- **Pouring behavior is less predictable:** Discharge may be plug-like or may produce rat-holing and intermittent flow, making the depth-to-line-position mapping unreliable without calibration (hogg2009mixingandsegregation pages 4-5).

### 5. SEM-EDS Statistical Requirements

For detecting a composition difference Δ (in wt% Si) between layer samples using per-particle SEM-EDS:

**Recommended particle counts:** BS ISO 13322-1:2014 and NIST recommend measuring approximately **10,000 particles** for statistical robustness of morphological descriptors (balart2022automatedsemedsanalysis pages 6-10). Automated SEM-EDS systems such as AutoEMX typically collect ~100 EDS spectra per sample (giunto2026accuratesemedsquantification pages 3-5). For the user's current protocol of ~30 particles per sample, a standard two-sample t-test power analysis applies:

n = 2(z_(α/2) + z_β)² σ² / Δ²

where σ is the per-particle standard deviation of Si content, α is the significance level, β = 1 − power, and Δ is the minimum detectable difference. For AlSi10Mg (nominal ~10 wt% Si), if the per-particle standard deviation σ ≈ 1–2 wt% Si (a reasonable estimate for single-particle EDS on well-alloyed spherical particles), then:

- To detect Δ = 2 wt% Si with 80% power at α = 0.05: n ≈ 2 × (1.96 + 0.84)² × (1.5)² / (2)² ≈ **18 particles per sample** (for σ = 1.5 wt%).
- To detect Δ = 1 wt% Si: n ≈ **70 particles per sample**.
- To detect Δ = 0.5 wt% Si: n ≈ **280 particles per sample**.

The user's 30 particles per sample is therefore adequate to detect ~1.5–2 wt% Si differences but insufficient for sub-1 wt% resolution. Increasing to ≥50 particles per sample, or ideally ≥100, would substantially improve sensitivity. For the number of samples (depth locations), Muzzio et al. (1997) showed that N = 30 random samples gave a poor estimate of the true composition distribution F(c), while N ≥ 100 samples gave close approximations (muzzio1997samplingpracticesin pages 14-16). For the user's three-point depth profile (top, middle, bottom), three samples is the minimum for detecting a monotonic drift; five or more depth points would allow assessment of nonlinear trends. Replicate samples at each depth (≥3 replicates) are essential to distinguish real drift from sampling noise.

### 6. Recommendation

For the user's specific scenario—small batches (5–100 g) of 15–63 µm cohesive aluminium alloy powder in a narrow stainless tube—**Method 4 (layer-by-layer removal with a spatula or spoonula)** is the best-supported approach. It avoids all probe-insertion artifacts, and cohesion helps preserve the exposed surface. Divide the powder into at least three depth fractions by removing full cross-sectional layers, weighing each. For each fraction, analyze ≥50 particles by SEM-EDS to detect Si differences of ~1 wt%. If physical access to the tube interior is limited, **Method 2 (piston corer)** with a large-bore, polished, thin-wall tube is the second-best option, but the core must be corrected for ~40% shortening and boundary slices discarded. Methods 1 and 3 introduce unacceptable drag-down for this application, and Method 5 requires tracer calibration before trust can be placed in the depth-to-position mapping.

A polished, pointed, gasketed design is better but still inferior to coring or peeling (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000014). | **Generally worst choice** for this objective; acceptable only after powder-specific tracer validation. |
| **4. Remove successive horizontal layers with spatula or spoonula** | **No insertion drag-down.** The principal error is local downward cutting or collecting slumped material from the newly exposed surface; no directly comparable quantitative value was reported. | None. No enclosed core means no wall-friction shortening or plugging. | Usually the smallest controllable smear if thin layers are shaved across the whole cross-section. Smear is set mainly by scoop penetration, surface roughness, and sidewall residue; avoid digging and exclude deliberate wall-brushings from the time series. Surface scooping can otherwise cause particles to flow down a slope and enrich fines (pqac-00000007). | **Best.** Directly maps removed mass or thickness to original depth, provided the container stays upright and each full cross-sectional layer is removed before the next. | Cohesion is beneficial because it suppresses slumping and percolation, although agglomerates and electrostatic adhesion require antistatic tools and gentle handling (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000043). | **Best overall for a shallow, accessible bed.** Prefer full-cross-section mass fractions over three isolated spoonfuls. |
| **5. Pour out while translating the container over a plate** | No probe drag, but discharge itself redistributes material. Funnel flow is only approximately first-in/last-out: central material moves first, wall material later, and material from different radii and heights can mix (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000023). | None, although cohesive powder may discharge in intermittent plugs or leave wall deposits, breaking the depth-to-position mapping. | Potentially broad. A flowing surface avalanche mixes neighboring layers; heap formation also causes fines to percolate inward while coarser particles roll outward (pqac-00000020). | **Unreliable without calibration.** The line records discharge time, not uniquely original depth; strict FIFO or LIFO should not be assumed. Final discharge can be disproportionately wall material (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019). | Cohesion may reduce size segregation and make plug-like discharge more order-preserving, but may instead cause clumps, rat-holing, intermittent release, and retained wall powder. Keep drop height and heap formation minimal (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000045). | **Third choice after peeling and piston coring.** Use only if tracer tests demonstrate a monotonic depth-to-line-position calibration for the actual tube and powder. |


*Table: Comparison of five methods for recovering chronological depth layers from a shallow cohesive powder bed. The evidence favors full-cross-section layer removal, followed by a calibrated piston corer.*

#### Method 1: Open Glass Tube, Thumb-Sealed

No published study uses this exact configuration. However, a glass core sampler (15 mm ID) pushed through a 150 mm lactose bed recovered only 60% of the insertion depth due to wall-friction plugging (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027). The axial stress required to continue filling the tube grows exponentially with depth and is determined by the wall friction coefficient μ_w and the Janssen K-ratio (pqac-00000026). When the tube is open during insertion, powder enters continuously from the bottom; wall friction drags upper material downward, compressing the core. Dividing the shortened core into equal thirds does not correspond to equal original bed depths. For cohesive 15–63 µm powder, the high surface-to-volume ratio increases wall adhesion, making plugging more severe.

#### Method 2: Piston Corer

The piston corer addresses the continuous-entry problem by holding a plunger at the powder surface while the tube is pushed down. This is mechanically similar to the core sampler tested by Susana (2012), which showed <10% contamination of upper-layer material 10 mm below a sharp interface—substantially better than side-sampling thieves (90%) or slug end-samplers (45%) (pqac-00000027). However, core shortening remains a concern: the 60% sampling efficiency measured for a 15 mm core tube means that a 40% compression of the core occurs. During extrusion, the stress required to push out the core can be double that developed during insertion (the exponent effectively doubles), further compacting the sample and potentially inducing reverse drag (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000028). For cohesive powder, wall adhesion a_w contributes an additional exponential term to the stress profile (pqac-00000026). Using a larger-diameter, polished, thin-wall tube reduces stress buildup substantially.

#### Method 3: Multi-Compartment Sampling Thief

The extensive experiments of Muzzio et al. (1997) demonstrate that all thief designs introduce significant errors in layered beds. A commercial side-sampling thief (Globe Pharma) produced samples that were "composed almost entirely of particles from the top layer regardless of whether the top layer was composed of smaller particles or larger particles," with maximum composition errors approaching 100% (pqac-00000013). Even particles entered the cavity before it was opened. The streamlined Rutgers end-sampling thief still showed ~10% composition error and contamination from particles originally 5–10 cm from the target location (pqac-00000014). The conventional side-sampling probe produced mixed-color sand within two aperture diameters (3.25 mm) of the layer boundary (pqac-00000013). For cohesive powders, an additional problem is that material may not flow readily into thief cavities, producing undersized or biased samples (pqac-00000012).

#### Method 4: Layer-by-Layer Removal with Spatula

This method avoids insertion drag entirely because no probe penetrates the bed. The principal errors are (i) cutting too deep, mixing the current layer with the one below, and (ii) surface segregation during scooping, where fines can percolate through coarser particles on a sloped surface (pqac-00000007). For the user's application (a tube a few cm across, total depth a few cm), removing full cross-sectional layers by careful horizontal scraping should give the best depth fidelity. Cohesion is beneficial here: it suppresses particle mobility, reduces slumping of exposed surfaces, and makes the exposed layer more stable (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000043).

#### Method 5: Pour-and-Sample Along a Line

Pouring powder from a container involves complex flow patterns. In narrow containers, discharge commonly follows a funnel-flow pattern, which is only approximately first-in-last-out: material near the center exits first while wall-adjacent material exits last (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019). Engblom (2012) found that discharge produced nearly constant fines content for most of the outflow, with strong composition changes only in the final material (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000021). Critically, pouring onto a surface creates a heap, and heap formation causes size segregation: fines percolate centrally while coarse particles roll outward (pqac-00000020). Surface avalanche flow mixes adjacent layers during deposition. The model for discharge segregation showed only moderate agreement with experiments (R² = 0.70) (pqac-00000022). For cohesive 15–63 µm powder, discharge may be plug-like (more order-preserving) but could also produce rat-holing or intermittent flow (pqac-00000045).

### 3. DEM Contact Models and Simulation Framework

While no DEM simulation has been published for sampling tool insertion into layered beds, the relevant framework is well established. The standard contact model is the **Hertz–Mindlin no-slip formulation**: normal forces depend nonlinearly on elastic overlap through the effective Young's modulus and effective radius (Hertzian contact), while tangential forces use Mindlin's incremental stiffness with Coulomb friction limiting (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000035). For cohesive powders, the **Johnson–Kendall–Roberts (JKR) model** is typically added to introduce adhesion, with pull-off forces proportional to surface energy and particle radius; this is implemented in common DEM packages such as EDEM 2.7.1 (pqac-00000031). The Rayleigh timestep criterion (typically 20–40% of the critical value) governs simulation stability (pqac-00000031). Practical DEM simulations can handle several hundred thousand to a few million particles (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030); for the user's application (a tube a few cm across containing ~5–100 g of 15–63 µm powder), the particle count would be on the order of 10⁶–10⁸, which is at the limit of current capability and would require coarse-graining (e.g., particle upscaling by a factor of 3–10, with adjusted contact parameters to preserve bulk behavior).

### 4. How Conclusions Change for Cohesive 15–63 µm Aluminium Powder

The user's powder spans a size range where interparticle cohesion becomes significant. Particles below ~20 µm are strongly cohesive, with dry-powder cohesion reducing individual-particle mobility and promoting agglomerate formation (pqac-00000045). For the full 15–63 µm distribution, the key changes relative to the literature experiments (which used free-flowing glass beads or lactose) are:

- **Reduced segregation:** Cohesion suppresses percolation and trajectory segregation mechanisms, meaning the as-deposited layering should be better preserved during storage (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000043). This is favorable for the user's objective.
- **Increased plugging risk in core samplers:** Wall adhesion a_w adds an exponential term to the stress buildup inside the probe, reducing sampling efficiency below the already-low 60% measured for lactose (pqac-00000026). A polished, large-bore stainless or PTFE-lined tube is advisable.
- **Thief cavity underfilling:** Cohesive powders may not flow into thief cavities, producing undersized or unrepresentative samples (pqac-00000012).
- **Layer-by-layer removal is more stable:** Cohesion prevents the exposed surface from slumping or self-segregating, making spatula removal the most reliable method (pqac-00000042).
- **Pouring behavior is less predictable:** Discharge may be plug-like or may produce rat-holing and intermittent flow, making the depth-to-line-position mapping unreliable without calibration (pqac-00000045).

### 5. SEM-EDS Statistical Requirements

For detecting a composition difference Δ (in wt% Si) between layer samples using per-particle SEM-EDS:

**Recommended particle counts:** BS ISO 13322-1:2014 and NIST recommend measuring approximately **10,000 particles** for statistical robustness of morphological descriptors (pqac-00000040). Automated SEM-EDS systems such as AutoEMX typically collect ~100 EDS spectra per sample (pqac-00000024). For the user's current protocol of ~30 particles per sample, a standard two-sample t-test power analysis applies:

n = 2(z_(α/2) + z_β)² σ² / Δ²

where σ is the per-particle standard deviation of Si content, α is the significance level, β = 1 − power, and Δ is the minimum detectable difference. For AlSi10Mg (nominal ~10 wt% Si), if the per-particle standard deviation σ ≈ 1–2 wt% Si (a reasonable estimate for single-particle EDS on well-alloyed spherical particles), then:

- To detect Δ = 2 wt% Si with 80% power at α = 0.05: n ≈ 2 × (1.96 + 0.84)² × (1.5)² / (2)² ≈ **18 particles per sample** (for σ = 1.5 wt%).
- To detect Δ = 1 wt% Si: n ≈ **70 particles per sample**.
- To detect Δ = 0.5 wt% Si: n ≈ **280 particles per sample**.

The user's 30 particles per sample is therefore adequate to detect ~1.5–2 wt% Si differences but insufficient for sub-1 wt% resolution. Increasing to ≥50 particles per sample, or ideally ≥100, would substantially improve sensitivity. For the number of samples (depth locations), Muzzio et al. (1997) showed that N = 30 random samples gave a poor estimate of the true composition distribution F(c), while N ≥ 100 samples gave close approximations (pqac-00000015). For the user's three-point depth profile (top, middle, bottom), three samples is the minimum for detecting a monotonic drift; five or more depth points would allow assessment of nonlinear trends. Replicate samples at each depth (≥3 replicates) are essential to distinguish real drift from sampling noise.

### 6. Recommendation

For the user's specific scenario—small batches (5–100 g) of 15–63 µm cohesive aluminium alloy powder in a narrow stainless tube—**Method 4 (layer-by-layer removal with a spatula or spoonula)** is the best-supported approach. It avoids all probe-insertion artifacts, and cohesion helps preserve the exposed surface. Divide the powder into at least three depth fractions by removing full cross-sectional layers, weighing each. For each fraction, analyze ≥50 particles by SEM-EDS to detect Si differences of ~1 wt%. If physical access to the tube interior is limited, **Method 2 (piston corer)** with a large-bore, polished, thin-wall tube is the second-best option, but the core must be corrected for ~40% shortening and boundary slices discarded. Methods 1 and 3 introduce unacceptable drag-down for this application, and Method 5 requires tracer calibration before trust can be placed in the depth-to-position mapping.

contexts.context: Thief sampling can disturb a static or layered powder bed during insertion, causing interparticle movement, segregation, and contamination of lower bed regions by material from upper layers. Insertion may compact the powder and restrict flow into the sampling chamber, while particle attrition and pressure differences with sampling depth add further error. Sampling bias can also arise from preferential entry of larger, better-flowing excipient particles, electrostatic or size differences, free-flowing particles entering before the probe is opened, and particles becoming trapped around or in the chamber. Consequently, sample results may vary with depth, probe type, chamber orientation, and insertion angle. A core sampler is intended to isolate an undisturbed cylindrical core, and cohesive powders can remain in the tube, but its insertion disrupts powder outside the sampler and its removal further disturbs the surrounding bed. Multiple core locations should therefore be inserted before any sampler is withdrawn, and sampling locations should be separated by at least five core diameters when using a capping device, or two without it, to limit interaction between disturbed regions. These effects are particularly important in layered beds because disturbance and material displacement can mix or redistribute layers and compromise representativeness.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies several problems associated with thief sampling of powder blends. A unit-dose sample collected with a thief may not represent the whole batch because the thief can introduce sampling bias, particularly when attempting to obtain very small samples from a blender or transport drum. Reported consequences include lower measured drug content in thief samples than in corresponding tablets and greater apparent variability in blend samples. The text also distinguishes sampling error from actual blend nonuniformity: high between-location variation suggests poor blend uniformity, whereas high within-location variation suggests sampling error. Subsequent segregation during handling further limits the ability of blend samples to characterize the original powder mixture. The proposed alternative is stratified sampling of in-process dosage units from locations at greater risk of content-uniformity failure, which can reduce thief-related and weighing errors and improve detection of segregation after blending. This excerpt does not discuss a core sampler specifically, nor does it explicitly describe how either sampler disturbs layered powder beds. It only indicates that sampling and subsequent handling can cause or obscure segregation, so conclusions about core-sampler behavior or layer disturbance require another source.

It does establish the main powder-bed mechanisms that can affect either sampling method. Sampling can be nonrepresentative if the blend has segregated before or during sampling, since segregation is driven by particle-size and density differences, particle shape, friction, moisture, container characteristics, and powder movement. Disturbance from inserting or withdrawing a sampler would be relevant insofar as it causes vibration, stirring, rearrangement, or local movement of the bed. In a disturbed layered bed, larger particles tend to rise while smaller particles sink, independent of density; segregation is concentrated mainly in the upper 15 cm. Thus, a sampler that disrupts or selectively accesses layers may collect different size or composition fractions rather than the local bulk blend. The excerpt also notes that segregation can develop during handling, storage, transport, and sampling, and that it can produce variations in bulk density, chemical composition, tablet or capsule weight, and content uniformity. Layer loading or narrow compartments can reduce bed segregation, but the text does not specify how thief and core sampler geometries differ in their disturbance or bias.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies several sources of sampling bias and disturbance in powder-blend thief sampling. Probe insertion can compact the powder bed, so the withdrawn core may be shorter than the theoretical volume and may not represent the original local composition. This compaction is quantified by sampling efficiency, the ratio of sampled-core length to insertion depth. In a conventional core sampler (CS), the critical stages are filling during insertion, withdrawal, and emptying; high consolidation stresses can develop, especially during filling and extraction. Wall friction and powder-wall adhesion transmit shear into material beside the probe, producing axial drag and potentially moving material across originally distinct regions or layer interfaces. This is particularly significant in layered beds, where the study used contrasting white lactose and dark cocoa layers to quantify cocoa dragged into the lactose region. The CS also requires piston-driven core extraction, which can create further drag and residual stresses and disturb the sampled structure. The SCS design reduces these errors: its slide-and-cover construction permits the core to be detached by gently tapping the slide before removal, avoiding additional drag and preserving structure. Nevertheless, drag remains possible in both CS and SCS, while SCS geometry, including corners, can create localized narrow confinement and stress buildup. The excerpt does not quantify blend segregation or analytical error beyond these mechanical disturbances.
contexts.question: What are the biases, errors, and disturbances associated with thief sampler and core sampler when sampling powder blends? How do they disturb layered powder beds?

First, the material recovered by a conventional thief may not represent the concentration at the intended sampling location because powder from other regions contaminates the sample as the probe is inserted. This is especially relevant to spatially heterogeneous or layered beds, where probe penetration can mix or transfer material between layers and thereby obscure the original local composition. Instead, it reports that the groove sampler and core sampler were selected for the study because they were found to be more effective, accurate, and reliable than typical side- or end-sampling thieves. contexts.context:
Traditional thief samplers can produce biased, nonrepresentative measurements of blend uniformity because their insertion and filling operation disturbs the powder bed. Their cavities open after insertion, allowing powder to flow into them; this intrusion displaces material, creates friction against the probe walls, transmits stresses into the surrounding bed, and generates shear. Consequently, the original structure—particularly any spatial layering—may be rearranged or disrupted, while flow into the cavities can alter the material collected and the apparent mixing degree. The excerpt identifies both external drag on the probe and internal drag within the sampler as sources of disturbance.

The Core Sampler (CS) reduces external drag because it isolates a cylindrical core rather than relying on cavities filling from flowing powder. However, it is not free of error: insertion can deform and compact the sampled core, biasing its composition and spatial profile. Powder displacement and compressive stresses may become large enough to block the probe, preventing complete filling and causing an incomplete or nonrepresentative sample. The CS may therefore disturb layered beds through compaction and deformation even while preserving more of the surrounding structure than a conventional thief. The Sliding Cover Sampler was developed to reduce these effects by sequentially inserting its slide and cover, lowering radial and axial stresses, drag, and compaction.

contexts.context: Muzzio et al. immobilized a two-color 60-mm glass-bead mixture, sliced it into 10-mm sections, and analyzed composition by image patches (0.56×0.96 mm). The 3D database contained 820×105 cells; patch measurement error was at most 9.4%. Random sampling showed N=30 samples poorly estimated the composition distribution, whereas N=100 or 1000 improved it. Increasing sample size from 1 to 9 patches narrowed distributions; with 7,500 samples of nine patches, N=30–1000 estimates closely matched the true distribution. The authors conclude that “a larger number (>100) of small samples” is preferable when samples are undisturbed.

A blunt slug thief dragged upper particles deeply downward; only five independent samples were possible, with ~20% composition errors and 8% sample-weight RSD. contexts.context: The excerpt presents statistical mixing theory, not specific DEM or sampling-tool tests. Danckwerts’ spatial correlation is \(R(\rho)=\langle[C(r)-C_{av}][C(r+\rho)-C_{av}]\rangle/\langle[C(r)-C_{av}]^2\rangle\), with segregation scale \(S=\int_0^\infty R(\rho)d\rho\) and intensity \(I=s^2/s_0^2\). For random mixtures, composition samples are uncorrelated; averaging neighboring sub-units reduces variance by the number of units and approaches a Gaussian distribution. Figure examples compare \(N=30\) versus \(N=300\) samples and individual units versus 9-unit composite samples. The text notes proposed guidelines of \(N\ge30\), but warns real, incompletely mixed systems require case-specific sampling.

contexts.context: The excerpt distinguishes between mass-flow and funnel-flow discharge in silos and emphasizes that the discharge pattern affects the segregation observed during emptying. Mass flow is defined as movement of the entire silo contents whenever the silo is emptied, and it can be achieved with steep, low-friction hopper walls, provided arching does not obstruct the outlet. The excerpt does not include the subsequent description of funnel flow, so it does not explicitly establish whether funnel flow produces a first-in-last-out discharge sequence. Likewise, it does not provide direct evidence about how well vertical layers formed while powder is poured are preserved during discharge. The earlier sections describe several filling-stage segregation mechanisms—embedding, fluidization, and air-current effects—that can create vertical or horizontal concentration patterns before emptying. Therefore, the available text supports the conclusion that pouring and discharge flow must be considered together when evaluating segregation, but it is insufficient to determine the precise discharge order or the degree to which vertical layering remains intact.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes silo discharge rather than simple pouring from an open container. The investigated silo was intended to have funnel flow in the upper hopper and mass flow in the lower hopper, but the authors judged that it actually discharged in expanded flow because the fluidization plates did not create mass flow throughout the silo. Visual inspection showed that material near the upper hopper walls discharged last. This is consistent with funnel-flow behavior: material in central regions moves toward the outlet earlier, while material near the walls remains behind and is discharged later, producing an approximate first-in-last-out tendency for some regions rather than perfect chronological layering. The experiments showed that fine particles accumulated preferentially near the silo walls during filling and that the final material discharged contained substantially more fines. In the large-scale tests, the last roughly five to ten tons for product L1 and the last one to two tons for L4 were considered segregated. Thus, vertical or spatial layering is not necessarily preserved uniformly during discharge. Material can segregate laterally during filling, and the non-mass-flow pattern can leave wall-adjacent material until the end. In a true mass-flow silo, material from different radial positions at the same fill level would remix at the outlet, reducing abrupt end-of-discharge segregation; funnel or expanded flow preserves spatial differences more strongly.

contexts.context: The excerpt discusses silo discharge rather than the detailed flow pattern created when powder is initially poured from a container, so it does not establish a single pouring pattern. It distinguishes mass flow, in which the entire silo contents move, from funnel flow, in which stagnant or dead regions remain while material flows through a channel. Funnel flow is commonly associated with more severe segregation, but describing it simply as “first-in-last-out” is explicitly identified as an oversimplification; the actual withdrawal order depends on the flow geometry and material behavior. Regarding preservation of layers, vertical top-to-bottom segregation—such as fine particles accumulating in upper layers during filling—is not necessarily eliminated during mass-flow discharge and may remain at discharge. Thus, vertical layering can be preserved relatively well, particularly when the segregation is aligned vertically. By contrast, horizontal or side-to-side segregation is often reduced in mass flow because material from different radial positions is mixed at the outlet, although velocity gradients near the end of emptying can limit this remixing. Funnel flow generally does not correct radial segregation because different regions remain stagnant or move at different velocities.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a conical heap and hopper filling pattern rather than explicitly naming funnel flow. As powder is poured onto a heap, a high velocity gradient develops near the surface. Fine particles percolate toward the relatively stationary central region, while coarse particles roll down the outside toward the walls. In a hopper, this produces coarse material near the walls and a fine-material central core. During discharge, the fine particles are released first, followed by the coarse particles rolling down the inverted cone. Thus, the passage documents a discharge sequence associated with heap formation and segregation, but it does not establish a universal first-in-last-out rule for all funnel-flow conditions. It also indicates that pouring causes vertical or spatial size separation rather than preserving the original layering of granular material. The text emphasizes that heap formation is the most frequent cause of size segregation and recommends keeping the powder-bed surface level during filling or reducing the cross-sectional area to minimize it. The excerpt does not quantify how well vertical layers are preserved, nor does it directly compare funnel flow with mass flow. Its evidence instead suggests that pouring substantially rearranges particles according to size, with fines concentrating centrally and coarse particles migrating outward and downward.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes both funnel-flow and mass-flow behavior in silo experiments, rather than a simple container-pouring test. In funnel flow, material near the center moves toward the outlet while material near the walls can remain relatively stationary until later; thus, funnel flow can produce a broadly first-in/last-out tendency for regions near the walls, but the discharge is not a perfectly discrete first-in-last-out sequence. The reported results indicate mixing of bulk solids from different radial positions during discharge, producing a fairly uniform fines content for much of the outflow. However, material distribution near the upper hopper section remains important: the final discharge composition is influenced by the initial distribution there, and fines may increase sharply near complete emptying, particularly when segregation occurred during filling. The excerpt also shows that vertical layering or segregation is not necessarily preserved intact during pouring or discharge. Radial redistribution and flow can partially mix the material, while surface shape, filling history, free-fall distance, particle properties, and segregation strength affect the outcome. For M4, initially uniform material and the absence of apparent sifting produced nearly constant fines content. Strongly segregated mixtures such as M8 and M9 showed increasing fines toward the end, although the timing and magnitude differed. Therefore, vertical compositional structure may influence discharge order, but it is modified rather than simply preserved.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide a statistical power analysis or a formal sample-size calculation for determining how many particles must be measured by SEM-EDS to detect a composition difference between samples. It describes the authors’ practical acquisition scheme: each analyzed zone consists of 20 images per polished section and typically contains approximately 10,000 particles. Magnification is selected so that the probability of analyzing coarser particles exceeds 50%, and particle-by-particle elemental compositions are measured for mineral identification. The method assumes that mineral surface and volume distributions are equivalent and notes that multimineral particles are not included. Therefore, the reported approximately 10,000 particles is an operational dataset size used in this study, not a generally justified minimum number or a power-based requirement. To calculate the required number of particles for a comparison between samples, additional inputs would be needed: the expected composition difference or effect size, particle-to-particle variance, significance level (alpha), desired statistical power, and whether particles are independent or clustered by sample/image. Because particles from the same sample may not be statistically independent, the number of independent samples or sections should also be distinguished from the number of measured particles.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide a statistical power analysis, a formal sample-size calculation, or a stated number of particles per sample required to detect a composition difference between samples using particle-by-particle SEM-EDS. It instead documents measurement repeatability and acquisition conditions. Three identical SEM-AFA scans were performed on a fly-ash stub, with 90 particles successfully matched across all scans after edge-associated particles were removed. Morphological repeatability was high, with coefficients of variation of 0.71% for diameter, 1.47% for area, and 1.05% for perimeter. For EDS, the live time was approximately 5 seconds per particle, and particle counts ranged from 11,000 to 32,000, averaging 16,500 counts. Increasing live time from three to five seconds improved count levels and reduced variation, thereby improving elemental measurement statistics. These results can inform variance and measurement-error estimates for a future power calculation, but they are insufficient to determine the required particles per sample. Such a calculation would require the expected composition difference or effect size, within- and between-sample variability, significance level, desired power, and the statistical model or test planned for the particle-level EDS data.

contexts.context: Experiments on cohesive powders found conventional 15-mm core samplers only 60% efficient (SD 1.67), due to consolidation/plugging and possible reverse drag during core withdrawal. Slotted/structured samplers (SCS) achieved 82–95% efficiency; the 10-mm semi-cylindrical probe reached 95% (SD 0.67), while triangular probes reached 85–87%. At 10 mm below a sharp interface, upper-material contamination was 6–12% for SCS, <10% for core samplers, versus 45% for slug and 90% for side samplers. Semi-cylindrical geometry reduced drag versus triangular designs, especially by eliminating high-friction acute corners; extraction without core movement avoided upward contamination.

For cohesive powders, the core-sampler analysis predicts wall adhesion/friction causes drag and consolidation during insertion:  
“\(d\sigma_{zz}/dz=(4/D)\tau_w\)” and \(\sigma_{zz}\) rises exponentially with fill depth. Small diameter/high wall friction can increase stresses by 1–2 orders of magnitude and cause plugging. Piston extraction imposes further uniaxial compression; its stress exponent doubles, potentially generating much larger wall shear. In a 150-mm, four-layer lactose/cocoa bed, a 15-mm glass core sampler visibly increased drag/compaction and achieved only 60% efficiency (SD 1.67; three tests), versus 85–95% for improved thief geometries.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports that conventional core samplers (CS) cause high consolidation/compression, negatively biasing concentration versus depth, and may introduce “reverse drag,” contaminating upper layers with lower material during core extraction. Sliding Cover Samplers (SCS), developed for cohesive powders, use two thin shells inserted sequentially to envelop static material, minimizing bed stress, movement, segregation, and drag. Contact mechanics use a simplified Hertz–Mindlin–Deresiewicz formulation, referred to as the TM model. During unloading, the previous tangential contact force is rescaled because the decreasing contact area reduces tangential stiffness; failing to rescale it can introduce spurious energy. The model was implemented in MultiFlow and used in the DEM simulations reported in the work. Time integration is explicit and uses the Verlet algorithm: forces and torques update half-step translational and rotational velocities, which then update particle positions and orientations. Stability requires a time step below the critical value, with a commonly suggested estimate based on the minimum particle mass and maximum spring constant. The excerpt also notes that critical time-step selection depends on particle arrangement, polydispersity, and coordination number. Collision detection uses linked cells and periodic-boundary ghost cells, with nominal O(N) complexity. This approach becomes inefficient for strongly polydisperse systems because cell sizes must accommodate the largest particle. Hierarchical grids are proposed as a more efficient alternative, but were not implemented in MultiFlow for the relatively small, weakly polydisperse systems considered.

contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that interparticle cohesion—particularly among cohesive fine particles—reduces flowability because adhesive forces strongly influence particle motion. Such poorly flowing fines contribute to segregation when mixed with particles having different sizes, densities, cohesion levels, or shapes. The text does not specifically identify a 100-micron threshold or quantify the effect of van der Waals forces, but the described adhesive-force behavior is consistent with the increasing importance of surface forces as particles become finer. Cohesive fines can resist movement, form agglomerates, and respond differently from coarser particles during handling, thereby promoting demixing and reducing mixture uniformity. These effects also complicate sampling: segregation and poor flow may cause a thief probe to encounter nonrepresentative material, which is why the excerpt discusses characterizing probe drag and sampling efficiency. During granulation, sampling is used to assess bulk composition, binder-spreading homogeneity, and nucleation/growth. Overall, stronger cohesion is expected to impair granular flow, increase the tendency of fine particles to adhere or agglomerate, and make mixing and representative sampling more difficult. contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that strong interparticle cohesion is especially important for very fine, soft, or irregular particles, including particles smaller than approximately 20 µm. In fluidization, cohesion can prevent uniform bed expansion: gas forms channels while much of the powder remains stagnant, and plugging or channeling occurs. For mixing, cohesion promotes agglomeration and can prevent individual particles from separating and redistributing. Sufficient energy is needed to break cohesive forces within aggregates; otherwise, low-energy mixers may blend agglomerates rather than individual particles, producing nonuniformity. Interactive mixing can improve homogeneity when fine drug particles adhere to larger carrier particles, creating stable ordered mixtures. However, segregation remains possible if adhered fine particles detach (constituent segregation), or if interactive units differ in size and undergo percolation or trajectory segregation. The excerpt also identifies percolation, densification, vibration, gravity, and particle acceleration as segregation mechanisms in random mixtures. It does not directly discuss sampling error or explicitly identify van der Waals forces. Nevertheless, its description of adhesion and cohesion provides relevant context: attractive interparticle forces generally reduce granular mobility, hinder fluidization and free-flowing behavior, encourage agglomeration, and make representative mixing or sampling more difficult unless adequate mixing energy and handling controls are applied.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies interparticle cohesion as especially important for fine powder components, explicitly associating dry-powder cohesion with particles below approximately 20 microns. Cohesion restricts individual-particle mobility and therefore generally reduces the tendency of particles to segregate. However, this does not necessarily improve mixing: the reduced mobility of fines can compound segregation problems, particularly when larger particles remain mobile. During agitation, cohesive fine powders can form agglomerates, and these agglomerates may segregate readily from the bulk fine powder. Thus, cohesion can make the powder behave as a population of larger, less mobile aggregates rather than as independently flowing primary particles, which is relevant to mixing uniformity and sampling representativeness. The excerpt does not directly discuss sampling protocols, particles specifically below 100 microns, or van der Waals forces by name. It does indicate that cohesion associated with liquid phases can extend across a wider particle-size range and may sometimes help minimize segregation. In the context of fine powders, van der Waals attraction is therefore relevant only indirectly here: it would be expected to contribute to cohesive bonding and agglomeration, but the excerpt provides no explicit mechanism or quantitative description of its effect on granular flow.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not specifically quantify the effect of interparticle cohesion or van der Waals forces for fine particles below 100 microns, nor does it directly discuss sampling behavior. It does indicate that surface condition and particle shape influence powder flow and segregation. Irregular particles can entangle and interlock with neighboring particles, reducing free flow and limiting percolation, whereas particles with greater flowability form smaller repose angles and are more able to segregate. Particle shape also changes the surface-to-volume ratio and therefore modifies the influence of surface condition on particle movement. For sticky particles, interfacial adhesive force depends on contact area, which is itself determined by particle shape; this suggests that cohesion can alter particle mobility and segregation tendencies. The excerpt further emphasizes that segregation requires relative particle movement and can be induced by operations such as vibration, gravity-driven flow, and shear. However, it does not identify van der Waals forces by name or provide a specific size-dependent conclusion for sub-100-micron particles. Thus, the passage offers only indirect support for the relationship between cohesion, flowability, segregation, and mixing.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not directly discuss interparticle cohesion, van der Waals forces, or their specific effects on the segregation, sampling, and mixing of particles below 100 microns. It does identify 10–100 μm material as granular powder and states that particle size directly affects mobility and segregation behavior. It also classifies surface properties and electrostatic properties as internal particle factors that can contribute to segregation. For fine particles, these observations provide only general context: size-dependent mobility and surface-related properties may influence powder behavior, but the excerpt does not explain whether cohesion increases or suppresses segregation, how it alters sampling representativeness, how it affects mixing, or how van der Waals attraction changes granular flow. No mechanism linking van der Waals forces to flowability, agglomeration, arching, or cohesive powder transport is presented.
contexts.question: What is the effect of interparticle cohesion on powder segregation, sampling, and mixing behavior for fine particles below 100 microns? How does van der Waals force affect granular flow?

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: Context: We make small batches (roughly 5-100 g) of aluminium alloy powder (AlSi10Mg, and blends of Al 6063 with Al 4047, spherical, mostly 15-63 µm) by ultrasonic atomization. The powder falls through a cone into a collection container (a stainless tube a few cm across), so the first powder made ends up at the bottom and the last at the top; powder brushed off the chamber walls is added on top at the end. We want to know whether per-particle composition (mainly Si, measured by SEM-EDS on about 30 particles per sample) drifts during a run, for example because the melt was not fully mixed, so we need top, middle and bottom samples whose composition reflects their depth in the container. Particle size is not the target here; compositional homogeneity is.

Question: Using discrete element method (DEM) simulations and tracer or layered-bed experiments in the literature, how well do these sampling approaches preserve the vertical (time-of-production) layering of a shallow bed of fine, somewhat cohesive powder, and which is best?
(1) an open glass tube pushed to the bottom, closed with a thumb or stopper, lifted out and emptied in thirds;
(2) a piston corer (a plunger held at the powder surface while the tube is pushed down around it, then the core extruded in thirds);
(3) a commercial or 3D-printed multi-compartment sampling thief;
(4) removing layers one at a time with a spatula or spoonula;
(5) pouring the container out while moving it along a straight line over a plate, then sampling at intervals along the line, so that position along the line maps to depth in the container.
For each, what does the evidence say about smearing at layer boundaries, drag-down of upper layers by the inserted tool, core shortening or plugging from wall friction, and whether pouring preserves order (first in, last out; mixing in the surface avalanche)? Give quantitative values where reported (mixing indices, boundary smear width in particle diameters, sampling bias), the DEM contact models, particle counts and coarse-graining used, and say how the conclusions might change for cohesive 15-63 µm aluminium powder. Finally, how many particles per sample and how many samples are needed for SEM-EDS to detect a given Si difference between layers?

## Preservation of Vertical Layering During Sampling of Shallow Powder Beds: Evidence from Experimental Studies, DEM Frameworks, and Statistical Considerations

### 1. Overview and Literature Landscape

The question of how well sampling tools preserve the chronological (vertical) layering of a powder bed has been addressed most thoroughly in the pharmaceutical blending literature, where blend uniformity testing by thief probes is critical for regulatory compliance. The key experimental studies are by Muzzio et al. (1997), who quantitatively compared side-sampling, end-sampling, and streamlined probes using layered glass-bead beds solidified with gelatin (muzzio1997samplingpracticesin pages 7-8, muzzio1997samplingpracticesin pages 8-11, muzzio1997samplingpracticesin pages 11-14), and Susana (2012), who developed and tested a sliding-cover sampler (SCS) using stratified lactose–cocoa powder beds and measured both sampling efficiency and drag contamination (susana2012lowshearwet pages 114-119, susana2012lowshearwet pages 119-123, susana2012lowshearwet pages 123-128). Funnel-flow and mass-flow discharge order have been studied by Engblom (2012) using tracer objects and composition monitoring during silo emptying (engblom2012segregationofpowder pages 29-33, engblom2012segregationofpowder pages 69-72, engblom2012segregationofpowder pages 56-62). Cohesive powder behavior is reviewed by Hogg (2009) and Hickey et al. (2003) (hogg2009mixingandsegregation pages 2-4, hickey2003aguideto pages 74-78, hogg2009mixingandsegregation pages 4-5).

A notable finding of this literature search is that **no DEM simulation has been published that directly models the insertion of a thief or core sampler into a layered granular bed** and quantifies boundary smearing or drag-down in particle diameters. DEM studies of granular intruders (ploughs, indentation tools, probes) exist, using Hertz–Mindlin contact mechanics with JKR or linear cohesion models (behjani2018numericalsimulationof pages 79-83, pasha2013modellingofflowability pages 157-163, knight2019fluidflowand pages 77-82, knight2019fluidflowand pages 74-77), but they have not been applied to the sampling geometry. The quantitative data below therefore come entirely from physical experiments with tracer- or contrast-layered beds.

### 2. Quantitative Evidence for Each Sampling Method

The following table summarizes the key quantitative contamination and efficiency data from the literature:

| Sampler Type | Reference | Material System | Contamination metric | Value |
|---|---|---|---|---:|
| Globe Pharma commercial side-sampler | Muzzio et al. (1997) | Two layers of 60 and 200 µm glass beads | Maximum composition error; sample-mass variability | ≈100% error; 34% RSD (muzzio1997samplingpracticesin pages 7-8, muzzio1997samplingpracticesin pages 8-11) |
| Slug end-sampling thief | Muzzio et al. (1997) | Two layers of 60 and 200 µm glass beads | Maximum composition error; sample-mass variability | ≈30% error; 8% RSD (muzzio1997samplingpracticesin pages 7-8, muzzio1997samplingpracticesin pages 11-14) |
| Pointed Rutgers end-sampler | Muzzio et al. (1997) | Two layers of 60 and 200 µm glass beads | Composition error; sample-mass variability | ≈10–20% error; 6% RSD (muzzio1997samplingpracticesin pages 7-8, muzzio1997samplingpracticesin pages 11-14) |

| Streamlined pointed end-sampler | Muzzio et al. (1997) | Layered glass beads | Maximum original distance from target location of contaminating particles | 5–10 cm (muzzio1997samplingpracticesin pages 11-14) |
